utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-00-39-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Krajisnik if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask for the appearances for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I understand Mr. Krajisnik's counsel for JCE is not here, so for the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Peter Kremer and Katharina Margetts appearing as counsel for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager Alma Imamovic-Ivanov. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. And for the amicus curiae, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colin Nicholls assisted by Qunicy Whitaker. Sorry I repeat. Colin Nicholls, assist by Qunicy Whitaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, this is an evidentiary hearing on appeal in the case of the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. The purpose of the hearing is to hear the testimony of Mr. Nicholas Stewart, who has been called by the appellant, Krajisnik, as a witness under Rule 115 of the Rules. Let me briefly summarise the relevant evidence which has been admitted in this appeal, and then I will detail the order in which we will hear the witness testimony today. First in its decision of 20 August 2008, the public version of which was filed on 4 November 2008, the Appeals Chamber admitted into evidence under Rule 115 two statements, Exhibits AD1 and AD2 authored by George Mano and Stefan Karganovic, respectively. Both statements concern the conduct of Mr. Stewart as lead counsel during the appellant's trial. In its decision of 8 October 2008, the Appeals Chamber admitted seven documents presented by the Prosecution as rebuttal evidence to these statements, and that is Exhibits AP1 to AP7. On 4 November 2008, the Appeals Chamber heard the testimony of Mr. Mano and Mr. Karganovic in relation to their previously admitted statements. On 6th November 2008, the Appeals Chamber admitted into evidence under Rule 115 six other documents also relating to Mr. Stewart's conduct as counsel at trial, and that is Exhibits AD4 to AD9. In the same decision, the Appeals Chamber ordered the appellant to contact Mr. Stewart to appear before the Appeals Chamber as a witness pursuant to Rule 115. I would like to remind the parties and the amicus curiae that all the exhibits admitted on appeal are under seal. Therefore, if the parties or the amicus curiae wish to refer to these documents, they should request private session. We will proceed in the following manner this afternoon: First, the appellant will have one hour to conduct his examination-in-chief of Mr. Stewart. Then the amicus curiae may question Mr. Stewart for 30 minutes. After that we have a break. The Prosecution may cross-examine the witness for one hour, followed by the re-examination of Mr. Stewart by the appellant for 20 minutes. These times allotted to the parties are approximate and may, with leave of the Chamber, be varied if necessary. As usual, I wish to remind the parties that they are not obliged to use all the time allocated and that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions to the witness. Before we call the witness, let me address one procedural issue regarding the supplemental briefs the parties and amicus curiae are allowed to file on any impact of Exhibits AD1 and AD2, the rebuttal evidence and the viva voce evidence of Mr. Mano, Mr. Karganovic, and Mr. Karadzic. These briefs are due on 14 November 2008, and on 5 November 2008, the Appeals Chamber decided that they be filed in a consolidated filing which shall not exceed 7.500 words. In light of its decision to admit Exhibits AD4 to AD9, the Appeals Chamber hereby allows the parties and the amicus curiae to include arguments on any impact of these six exhibits and Mr. Stewart's testimony of today in the consolidated supplemental briefs. Also, we are still -- the Appeals Chamber extends the deadline for such consolidated filing until 18 November 2008, and expounds the word limit for this filing to a maximum of 9.000 words. That being said, I would now like to call witness Nicholas Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stewart. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, you may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, can you please tell the Court your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nicholas John Cameron Stewart, 16th of April 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And give us a brief indication of your previous and present occupations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a practising barrister at the bar of England and Wales and have been since 1972. I was appointed Queen's Counsel in 1987, and since 1992 or it may be 1991, I have been a deputy High Court Judge of the High Court of England and Wales, which is of course a part-time occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. You ever been summoned to testify in the appeal proceedings in the case of the Prosecutor against Momcilo Krajisnik. As it is the appellant, Mr. Krajisnik, who has called you to testify, he will conduct the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Afterwards, amicus curiae may question you followed the questioning by the Prosecution and finally you will be re-examined by the appellant. And please also note that the Judges may pose questions to you at any time of your testimony if they so wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I understand. That's very clear. May I -- Your Honour, may I ask two questions? I don't want to trespass on the appellant's or anybody's time. The first one, Your Honour, is this: That of course I'm aware that two witnesses gave evidence last Monday, and of course I know who they are because that was -- their identities were not kept secret; but a great deal of their evidence was heard in private session. If it's not impertinent of me, Your Honour, I wonder why because I want to make it clear that I seek no such privacy of anything for my own part, in my own interests. I would not have wished their evidence to be in private, nor do I wish any of my evidence so far as absolutely unavoidable to be in private. I would wish myself to give my evidence entirely in public and have as much as possible in public but I simply register that and I'm not sure, Your Honours, may I ask I'm not clear why such evidence was given in private if that's an appropriate question for me to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, as a witness you should be asked questions more than putting questions. In any event, most of the documents, all number of documents that have been examined by -- or used during the examination in the hearing you are mentioning were private documents, and inevitably all the references to this was to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you, Your Honour. That does answer the question then on the technical level, and Your Honours and everybody understands my position. Your Honour, my other question which I believe is an appropriate one for a witness, because I do wish to give what help I can, is I'm very unclear, and it seems to me that it may come up quite quickly where I currently stand in relation to privilege as regards Mr. Krajisnik and what I am and am not free to say as his former counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, this is a matter essentially for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Some of your -- may be covered by privilege. You should use your privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that case if the position is that there has been no change in where I always stood as far as privilege was concerned in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, then until anybody directs me otherwise, I shall respect that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. I wanted to ask the appellant if -- if he believes that the witness should stick to the -- to the privilege or not, I mean, because in a way it's up to you to waive it or not. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I was advised by Mr. Dershowitz and Mr. Sladojevic that I should not waive my privilege, and I am inclined to follow their advice since they are more knowledgeable on the matter than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. We take note of that. We take note of that, and of course you will take that into account in putting the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, of course, I've noted that specifically, naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems to me that the privilege belongs to the appellant, not to the lawyer normally, and if Mr. Krajisnik called Mr. Stewart to testify on a range of issues, on that range of issues it will be my sort of assumption that Mr. Krajisnik waived privilege; and the range of issues on which Mr. Krajisnik would want Mr. Stewart to testify are issues of ineffective assistance and unfair trial. So it seems to me that Mr. Krajisnik cannot have it both ways. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] My apologies. Can I take the floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, sure. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I was now advised by Mr. Sladojevic that the examination should go ahead and that if we should come at a stage where this right could be infringed, we will definitely make a decision on that matter. For the sake of respecting both the confidentiality and the privilege and the interest of the public, I will make a decision; but I would not wish to make it an obstacle to substantive testimony of Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. That's why I was saying earlier that you should -- or you will take into account how far you want to waive in putting the questions. But it is clear that if you put a question, the witness will answer the question, because it's obvious if you ask it's unavoidable that you are seeking an answer to the question you put. So can we agree on that? In that case, I give the floor to Mr. Krajisnik for the examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since I was caution by the Chamber that reference to -- to the documents calls for private session, I would therefore ask Their Honours to go into public [as interpreted] session for a short while because I will be referring to certain documents under seal.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: You mean private session?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Private session, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I should like to direct Mr. Stewart to the documents I hope you have with you, namely three documents, AD4, AD5, and AD6.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, may I make it clear I have brought nothing with me, nor do I know which documents the reference numbers you give refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask to give the witness these three documents mentioned by Mr. Krajisnik, AD4, AD5, and AD6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you. I have them. Well, I have three documents, Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is your letter to the Chamber with an enclosed memo and notes that you made during the -- your meeting with Judge Orie and Mr. Zahar. Did you have occasion to review the material before and are you familiar with the material? If not, you can have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, yes, I have the three documents. The letter with a fairly long memorandum attached to it, and then, yes, the note of my meeting with Judge Orie and the note of my meeting with Mr. Zahar. The answer is, yes, I have reviewed all of -- well, what looked like copies of these same documents. I have reviewed them carefully within the last 48 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Stewart, for Their Honours that these documents were authored by you, that you wrote them or participated in their drafting?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, I can. The -- the longer documents attached to the letter of the 28th of October and possibly some of the letter itself, but the longer document was actually drafted together with my co-counsel, Mr. Josse. I think we pretty much split it 50/50, but right now I wouldn't know exactly which bit came from which of us. But, yes, it's got my name on it of course. If it was sent -- signed by me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I'm happy with your answer. Is there anything in the documents that you would wish to correct at this time? You said that you have had occasion to remind yourself of the contents of the documents over the past 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. There are two very small corrections. I'm ignoring punctuation and things and so on, Mr. Krajisnik. There are two very small corrections. In the note of the meeting with Judge Orie, Monday, 31st of October, in the penultimate paragraph on the first page, the

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: And there's the -- the word "days" is missing the next page in the middle, but again I think that's pretty obvious but almost in the middle of the long paragraph it says, "NS was near the end of the 120," and that's a 120-day final cut-off but that's pretty trivial. Otherwise, Mr. Krajisnik, I haven't seen anything, and I could confirm that so far as these documents express opinions they are and remain my honest opinion and so far as they express facts, those facts are absolutely and completely true. Facts stated by me, assert by me, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Does this mean that you stand by the entire contents of the three documents? Is that a conclusion we can draw, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's correct, yes. I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to go back into open session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the beginning of my examination, I would like to briefly refer to the start of trial and the witnesses who were called at the time. If you remember, among others Madam Plavsic and Mr. Djeric were called. This is my question: Do you believe that the Trial Chamber allowed enough time, and that it was a fair amount of time for the examination of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Mr. Krajisnik said he briefly referred to the start of the trial. I don't think there's any dispute that Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Djeric were actually called right towards the very end of the -- of the trial hearing, but with that qualification. No, Mr. Krajisnik, I don't believe the Trial Chamber allowed enough time and that it was a fair amount of time. When one considers the amount of time which had been given to a number of other witnesses in the course of the trial and the very short allocation of time for these witnesses who certainly would have been expected, especially in the case of Mrs. Plavsic, to have far greater direct knowledge of the events with which the trial was concerned than many of those other witnesses, it seemed at the time to -- well, me and my co-counsel, there's no question about that, it seemed to us that it was really almost absurdly short amount of time to allocate for these witnesses, especially Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Does this mean that you did not have an appropriate amount of time for the examination of Madam Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, there are two points really, Mr. Krajisnik. Of course, knowing that we had a very short allocation of time, we naturally tailored what examination we were going to conduct to that time and didn't work out the cross-examination we would have gone in for it, we had had far longer time. But within the confines of what we were allocated and what we did attempt to cover, we will -- and, Mr. Krajisnik, I don't have detailed recollection of it, I believe the transcript itself will show that we felt ourselves to be cut off in the particular areas that we were wanting to pursue, especially in relation to, again without recall the details, Your Honours, extracts from Mrs. Plavsic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As for Mrs. Plavsic's book, the title of the book is, "I Testify." Was the book fully translated before you commenced the examination -- or, rather, before Mrs. Plavsic took the stand?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I don't believe it was, Mr. Krajisnik. My recollection, so far as it goes, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, do you recall in what manner the Trial Chamber during their examination of Mrs. Plavsic or to what extent they relied on her book and how certain paragraphs or excerpts from the book were selected?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honours, I do not recall this in detail, but interviews had been conducted with Mrs. Plavsic in Sweden by an officer from the Trial Chamber. I don't remember how far if at all the extracts of the book were particular content of those interviews which we were supplied with. I do just remember that it was what appeared to be a limited and, if you like, highly selective choice of specific points in Mrs. Plavsic's book. But I think just -- so your question is to what extent they relied. I -- from my recollection, but the transcript would show it, wouldn't it, I believe it was the Trial Chamber, she was a Chamber witness; it was the Trial Chamber who in effect relied upon those extracts. I think they took the initiative in -- in adducing that evidence as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, were you able to cross-examine Mrs. Plavsic in a satisfactory manner, particularly on the issue of her book entitled -- entitled "I Testify"?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, no I wasn't. I thought the whole exercise was unsatisfactory. There wasn't any -- it wasn't a serious opportunity for Mrs. Plavsic to be seriously examined I think either by the Prosecution or by the Defence as it happened, but so far as her -- the extracts from her book were concern, what I do -- what I do remember is that we were -- I think I've said we were rather cut off in trying to deal with this, and probably in trying to put the extracts from her book in context. But I rather think this would all be very clear from the transcript and there's nothing I could add to it. I don't believe I would have any recollection of that which would go beyond what's there on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stewart, that I wanted to examine Mrs. Plavsic, and you will recall that I was prevented from cross-examining her?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I do remember that, Mr. Krajisnik. And, Your Honours, I should say that this is the -- this is the one very limited piece of the transcript in relation to Mrs. Plavsic's evidence which I have reviewed; and I have reviewed it actually in the course of today because it was -- I don't think it would be any secret, Mr. Krajisnik. You and your team sent it to me to review. It's a quite short passage. But Mr. Krajisnik and Your Honours, I remember it very well, yes. It refreshed my memory, but I do have a very distinct memory. We made a submission which again is on the transcript. Our submission was that you were very peremptorily and unjustifiably cut off by Judge Orie from examining Mrs. Plavsic. And, Mr. Krajisnik, we know I say that as someone who wasn't a huge fan of your cross-examining our witnesses or any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to go back to the pre-trial period when you were appointed my counsel. When taking over the case, were you familiar with who had been my counsel before you? Can you tell us his name if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I remember that perfectly well. Your Honours, that was Mr. Brashich, Mr. Dan Brashich. I was told that straight away by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know or do you remember how long Mr. Brashich had been working on my case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. He'd been our case for -- well, some years. Two years, three years, four years maybe, but it was certainly a long time. You were arrested and brought here in April 2000; and as far as I recall, Mr. Brashich became your counsel quite soon after that. I don't remember exactly when, but not long after that, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, when you were taking over the case, did you expect to receive from Mr. Brashich a work product which would make it possible for you to put up a proper defence?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. What I was told by the -- the Registry, and of course it was true as far as it went, was that the trial had been due to begin I think it was on the 14th of May, but I don't think the exact date matters, that's a matter of record; but the trial had been due to begin on the 14th of May, and sometime toward the end of April it had come to light that Mr. Brashich either had been or was about to be disciplined and, in fact, then was disciplined and suspended from practice for a year and had to be taken off this case, but what I -- what I understood at the beginning was that -- well, just that, really, that the case had been two weeks away from trial in the hands of counsel who had been in the case for a long period, and whatever his deficiencies or defects which had led to him being suspended by the New York Bar, at that point I just assumed that the trial was -- I beg your pardon, your case was at the appropriate stage of preparation in the hands of your previous counsel for something that was due to start in two weeks', three weeks', four weeks' time. I became disabused of that eventually, but when I started that's what I understood. So, yes, I would have expected to receive a lot of materials useful for a trial from previous counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what material you did receive? Did you receive what you expected to receive from Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Mr. Brashich came here. It was arranged that he and I and my co-counsel being whom I'd brought into the case -- just brought into the case at that stage, Ms. Loukas from Australia; we met here for a week in August 2003, August 2003, and of course we came to see you, Mr. Krajisnik, as well. Mr. Brashich was supposed to bring papers, in fact that's one of the main purposes of his trip. The Registry paid for him to come. He was supposed to bring all the papers with him, and he didn't. He didn't bring anything apart from a few scraps of papers here and there. I eventually got papers out of him some two, three months later something like that, and it -- roughly speaking, it was 13 large packing cases of material from Mr. Brashich and 53 I think it was smaller boxes of papers from his co-counsel or one of his co-counsel Mr. Kostic came late autumn, something like that, after quite a struggle, and, no, it was in a -- it was a vast amount of material in a barely organised state. It was not at all what I had expected to receive when I started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, were you able to get an overview of what was in that documentation, because when embarking upon a case you have to know what is there so that you can organise your defence.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think what had clearly happened, and a certain amount of surmise here, Your Honours, because Mr. Brashich had been extremely resistant to sending these papers for quite a while and made some reference to needing some time and some help from his secretary. I think he had done some fairly hurried organisation. That was the impression I got of this material. So it was in sections. I was able in make -- I was able to make a list. I was able to make a schedule by broad category headings, but within those categories, and maybe there were 20 or 30 in each packing case, I wouldn't know precisely, Your Honours, but within each category it was pretty disorganised then. I also received, by the way, a fairly large number of CDs from Mr. Brashich and some old-fashioned floppies as well. Some of them had a few files on them. Some of them had a hundred files on. Some of them, I think, had a thousand or more files on them, but you had to go into the files and open them to find out what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, when you took over my case did you have a number of cases, ongoing cases, in London which you had to complete?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I had some work. I'm a practising barrister. Of course I -- well, I'm happy to say I didn't have no work, so -- so, yes, I did. And -- and naturally that was a point of discussion with the Registry. I -- it was -- of course I had to organise my work and wrap up what I could wrap up, release myself sufficiently to be able to do your case, yes. Although like, I would guess anybody, really, of course I wasn't able to close down every single bit of work I was doing; and I had obligations to -- obligations to clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I interrupt you a moment. Judge Meron, you wanted to put a question now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Stewart, you spoke of the problems arising from the fact in Mr. Brashich did not in fact hand over to you a significant work product.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And that you received all those boxes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, there was very little time at that time, and the amicus in his -- the redacted and public version of his brief pointed out to the fact that you chose not to seek a delay of the commencement of the trial. If that is correct, can you explain to the Bench the reasons for the decision not to ask for a delay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: In retrospect what effect do you think that had on your ability to provide Mr. Krajisnik with a full and adequate defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the simple point is that it is just not correct to say I did not seek a delay of the commencement of the trial. I struggled as hard as I could and fought as hard as I could to seek a commencement of the trial. What I didn't do, and I think this is very significant in the whole history of this, we didn't make a formal application to adjourn the trial because we had a number of meetings, I wouldn't know exactly how many again, but we had meetings with the senior trial officer, that was Mr. Harhoff at the time, of course Judge Harhoff now, we had meetings with Judge Orie. It was usually with Judge Orie alone, as far as I remember, rather than with all three Judges, and these matters were vigorously ventilated, and we -- I made it very clear to -- certainly to Mr. Harhoff, I made it clear to him in absolute penny numbers the position we were in and the state we were in; and I made that very clear to Judge Orie. But the bottom line is that we were trying to negotiate, and that continued for quite a long while, really, as a way of dealing with it; but I, at one point in the discussions, I absolutely, and this I remember verbatim, Judge Orie just said to me in one of these meetings, "Mr. Stewart, this trial will start on the 3rd of February." Or the 4th, perhaps it was. Whatever the Monday was. And then that was it, "It will start." And actually, Your Honours, I believed him. It was very clear to me that Judge Orie meant that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And what significance did this all have on the adequacy of the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, what happened again, and this obviously dictated our approach as to whether we made a formal application, the trial didn't start -- I think it was the 4th actually, but the trial didn't start on the 4th of February and then just crack on five days a week. The discussions -- Judge Orie offered us a schedule where we were to have I think it was 18, again I'm speaking from memory and Your Honours will appreciate this is a few years ago; and I haven't read up on all this, but we were offered I think 18 days with some flexibility as to how we would structure that, whether we would have six weeks at three days or so on, so many weeks at four days and so on. We were offered flexibility on that on the understanding that when we had got those 18 days, I think it was, out of the way there would then be an adjournment; and it was until after Easter, which is around the 10th or the 11th of April. And although it was very difficult, in the light of what Judge Orie had said, "This trial will start," and in light of what he had offered us, I considered that an application for a more extensive adjournment at that point would be pretty much futile, as it happens. And I did think that we could cope anyway, and it would be of some value to us, actually, in getting to an unfamiliar Tribunal and getting to know the ropes and getting the feel. The understanding was that crime base witnesses would be produced at that point that ought to be manageable. The only thing that did happen in particular in those 18 days which made things rather more difficult was the calling Mr. Deronjic, but we did oppose that. We did resist that, unsuccessfully, but we did object to that. That was a different matter. Of course that was all connected with Mr. Deronjic facing his sentencing hearing and it became we thought slightly unsatisfactory. Judge Orie was also the Presiding Judge of the Chamber dealing with Mr. Deronjic's sentencing hearing. So we -- we -- there was quite a lot of discussion about the order of events, the Defence. We wanted Mr. Deronjic sentenced before he gave evidence. It was clear the Trial Chamber wanted it the other way around. We lost that particular skirmish about Mr. Deronjic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I put you one question, Mr. Stewart. You said that you had these meetings essentially only with Judge Orie. At the same time you said also you considered a formal application for adjournment or for delay in starting the trial would have been futile in light of the strong, firm position of Judge Orie. Didn't it jump to your mind that perhaps a formal application would have involved the other two Judges on the Bench, and they may have had a different opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course it crossed me mind but it didn't alter my conclusion, no. Throughout this case and I don't mean any disrespect to the other Judges, of course, there was a change of Judge as well; but throughout this case it was very clear and Mr. Harhoff is a very experienced senior trial officer of course was literally metaphorically sitting at Judge Orie's elbow, it was very clear to us that Judge Orie was effectively running that side of things. Or if it wasn't a fact, that was our judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I take note of your judgement. Judge Guney, you wanted to ask something at this point. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, an additional question to the question of Judge Meron. Considering that you were assigned as lead counsel to the defence of Mr. Krajisnik on the 30 July 2003 and that you received the case matter in a disorderly state and with delay from the former counsel, Mr. Brashich, would you and could you say that you were enough prepared to start the trial of Mr. Krajisnik on the 3rd February 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, no, we weren't in the sense that it -- we felt, in fairness, the trial -- the whole trial should not have been started as soon as that; but we had made our representations, and subject to what I've said about Mr. Deronjic, I will say, Your Honours, that it was not actually at that point of the trial in February that we found ourselves significantly hampered. Those witnesses that -- apart from Mr. Deronjic, those witnesses that we dealt with in that first run of evidence over that 18-day period or whenever it was, were, we felt at the time with hard work and difficulty, were manageable. And again our consideration as to whether to keep fighting further and whether to make a formal application for an adjournment had to be viewed in the light of the fact that it was -- and I don't mean this in any disparaging way, Your Honours, but it was quite a -- it was quite a clever, well-thought-out offer that the Trial Chamber were giving us to have this -- just this early chunk of a limited number of days with our being offered some flexibility as to what the sitting pattern would be with then some adjournment. Because actually one effect of it was that Mr. Treanor gave his evidence-in-chief during that first batch of days, so his evidence-in-chief was concluded I think by the end of February 2004; but I didn't have to cross-examine him then until immediately after Easter, which was something like the 10th or the 11th. And although heaven knows, Mr. Treanor's report was vast and detailed and thorough and was an enormous challenge for us to get to grips with. I cross-examined Mr. Treanor; it was of course a help and an advantage to us to have had his evidence-in-chief some weeks before we had to cross-examine him. But those are always considerations came into play and others of course in considering whether in the light of this absolutely clear indication from Judge Orie whether there was any value in going the -- the formal convetive application route as opposed to continuing what I would call, if you like, the negotiation mode, which did in fact continue for quite some time over the first few months of the trial. We were not negotiating, we felt, with a very strong hand in the face of -- when I say that these matters -- by the way it occurs to me were run, if that was the phrase I used by Judge Orie, I'm talking as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, because we always had the very distinct impression that, that such questions as when this trial would start had an input and an influence and had pressures from beyond the Trial Chamber itself. That -- that seemed to us in all our conversations to be transparently obvious. I'm talking about New York. In loose terms I'm talking about New York, but perhaps I'm just using that as a label or metaphor for this institution in the light of the -- what turns out to have been the fairly appalling history of this case from the year 2000 through to 2003 and 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Mr. Stewart, you brought, I believe, a motion on the 22nd of February, 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Seeking an adjournment of the trial until the month of August of 2005. You wrote that you -- the current counsel, you described yourself as, that you had not read more than "15 per cent of the overall documents."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that -- Your Honour, may I be clear? I'm not -- of course, Your Honours, I'm not -- I'm not disputing that. I just want to be clear. We had -- we had brought a motion seeking an adjournment in July 2004. So Your Honour is now talking specifically about the second application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to be clear about that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You wrote that you by then you had not read more than 15 per cent of the overall documents in the case, and during the oral arguments on the 28th of February, 2005, your co-counsel, Mrs. Loukas, complained that there was an "inadequately developed defence strategy." Here is my question first: Could you please tell us if you were ever able to complete your review and analysis of the relevant material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, we weren't. We weren't, Your Honour. We -- we never did. It -- it -- we were never able to read all the papers, but on the other hand nor would I, of course, realistically suggest that any sensible lead counsel in any sensible conduct of any case would read a hundred per cent of the papers. After all heaven knows what if there is such thing as delegation apart from anything else and common sense sifting. So far as defence strategy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So before that would you say that this did not present a real problem that you did not cover more of the material in terms of efficacy of the defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that, Your Honours. With respect, that would be going too far the other way. For example, I had a -- I had a conversation with -- well, it was a semi-formal conversation. It wasn't a casual conversation on the balcony and so on but we, I think, had a conversation with Judge Harhoff, one of many meetings with him had, Mr. Harhoff as he was then, in which he would say and correctly he'd say, "Well of course there's all this paper, but we all know that when you have this sort of paper 60 per cent of it is completely irrelevant. " Well, I would say: "Well, yes, Fred, I agree with that but if you could kindly tell me which 60 per cent that would help us enormously and then we could simply concentrate on the other 40 per cent." I don't mean that in a flippant, jocular way. That to some extent was a real problem. Of course, one is able to identify with luck quite quickly stuff which is not really going to help, but it remained a problem, Your Honour, because we would never know - I don't want to sound like a particular politician - but we would never know what we didn't know. That's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And on the comment by Mrs. Loukas about the inadequate defence strategy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I wouldn't -- [B/C/S on English channel] sorry. Something happened. Never mind may I pick that up. I wouldn't myself stress that too much as a difficulty. The -- the broad lines of strategy in order to know what you were trying to do when you were cross-examining Prosecution witnesses were pretty clear, and I wouldn't whatever priorities I had set myself, I certainly wouldn't have entered into -- embarked upon cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses without at least working out what I was trying to achieve even if I had difficulties in being confident that I and my co-counsel were -- were able to lay our hands on all that might be relevant to help us achieve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, may I ask you to continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, now I would like to ask you to explore the topic of the time that the Defence had at its disposal during the trial, little time, lots of material. And now let me remind you of your motion of the 14th of July, 2004, where you state in paragraph 14 -- now you're talking about a lack of time that Their Honours have been asking you about, and you stress this problem that existed both before the trial began --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. You are talking -- Your Honours, Mr. Krajisnik, you're talking about the first application we made for a substantial adjournment, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me quote from this motion and then I will ask your comment. Two quotes. On the 14th of July, 2004, you said: "We are sure that the materials that the Prosecution has disclosed to us without the material under Rule 68 goes beyond 500.000 pages. What we know is this is voluminous material and we have been unable to examine the material let alone read it." In paragraph 15 of the same motion you say: "We have been unable to read and take into account in an appropriate manner all the materials pertaining to the witnesses who have already been cross-examined. We have often been presented with too much material and too little time. We will never be able to do that before the Prosecution case ends, and it will be too late at that stage." So my question to you is: Is this what you mean, and do you agree with me that the Defence team by July 2004 had not had enough time to prepare for trial?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what -- what -- what was said in -- in the paragraphs of the motion that you -- you quote was true. Now, in my tradition, of course, we make submissions as counsel. It doesn't mean that we will personally believe them. That's a different issue altogether. But of course when we're saying where we are in relation to our own preparation and our own handling of material, of course we are telling the Court our view, and we are telling the Court honestly where we stand, and that's what we were doing. So that was correct, Mr. Krajisnik, yes. We wouldn't have said it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Only the 16th of July, 2004, at page 4478 of the transcript you stated the following: "We simply cannot do everything. When we set our priorities from among six basic jobs, and we can only do two. We have come to the conclusion that we cannot defend Mr. Krajisnik in an appropriate manner. He knows it too. We know it too." And on the same day, the 16th of July, 2004, at page 4485 and 4486 of the transcript, you said in Court commenting on the huge pile of documents and the lack of time for the preparation, this is what you said: "I should not have underestimated this problem for such a long time, and I should not have ignored the problem as I have been doing at times. I should have warned the Trial Chamber promptly, and I wish I had done that, but I'm doing it now. We need time." Now, my question to you is this: Before this date did you warn the Trial Chamber that you did not have enough time and that there was voluminous material that you had to go through in order to be able to defend me as well as possible?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: On numerous occasions, Mr. Krajisnik. I wouldn't even know how many. The -- that message was conveyed loud and clear and had been for months and months and months, almost on every opportunity we had. It was certainly conveyed to Mr. Harhoff constantly. And really at any opportunity that we had, we reiterated it. Yes, that was loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 29th of October, 2004, at page 7668 of the transcript you state the following: "The problem is only exacerbated. We're at the breaking point as far as the Defence is concerned, because this team has been unable to manage no matter what it looked like on the surface. We could not have managed this trial efficiently up to now." Do you agree that in October 2004 the situation did not improve? By October 2004 the Defence team did not have enough time to prepare for the trial.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: What happened, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not attempting to sidestep your question at all, but I think that there are several points as there would be in a long trial which are critical, if you like. They're watershed points, and there was one in the summer of 2004 which led to that application, and it's to do with what I referred to earlier, which is, if you like, the negotiation mode of trying to achieve a manageable trial schedule and then moving to a different approach. We -- we had an extensive discussion with Judge Orie, and the Prosecution were there as well, of course, in one of these formal meetings, I suppose it was a 65 ter whether it was or it wasn't, it was in one of these rooms it was a formal meeting around the table to do with the exercise of attempting to achieve significant agreement of facts, and Judge Orie was prepared to give us weeks -- weeks possibly extending into months in return for our pledging to really try to have a significant batch of agreed facts with the Prosecution. Now, when I say negotiation mode, I rather mean that, Your Honours, because the language that Judge Orie used in these meetings was, "If you have such-and-such," and I mean this message being conveyed by us loud and clear about where we were and what we needed, Judge Orie would say and I remember this distinctly, "If we give you such-and-such, then it is going to cost me or cost us X days or X weeks." And I do remember. I don't believe it was disrespectful, it certainly wasn't intended to be, but we had fairly punchy exchanges in these meetings. I remember saying to Judge Orie, "Well, Judge, you know, with respect you sound like a banker," which was frankly less a tell of abuse than it might be now, but that was -- that was the way I put it, and it was true, really. It was -- now, of course I respect -- I sit as a Judge myself sometimes although I don't really have to manage that sort of problem, but of course you Judges with respect, of course, have the job of trying to make sure the case moves along. I understood that. You don't have inexhaustible resources, but that -- that trade-off was where we were. But what happened, and I put this in a nutshell now. We sweated blood to try to achieve that agreed facts. No doubt, Mr. Mano has told you all about it, but we sweated blood to try to agree facts. I had to push and drag a very reluctant team along on that at some point, but I saw it as my job to deliver if I possibly could what I had assured Judge Orie I would deliver, but in the end one weekend I thought very hard about where we were and how the Prosecution had far greater resources and far greater knowledge of what we were talking about; and my anxieties that we were letting ourselves drift into facts that it was not safe to agree because it was all provisional up to that point after all all these discussions about agreed facts, and I came to the conclusion one weekend that it was not in your interests, Mr. Krajisnik, to continue with this exercise. And I didn't believe I was in breach of duty to the Trial Chamber, because my duty to the Trial Chamber was to try and do my damnedest, which I did. Having done that I decided it was in your interest to pull the plug, which I did. Judge Orie was furious. He was absolutely furious. That was completely clear. Subsequent discussions I had with Judge Harhoff and we immediately switched back to what was going to be full trial mode then. Adjournment came to an end. Time came to an end. It was clear -- the recess was coming up of course, but it was clear we were going to crack on with this trial. At some point I said to Judge -- Mr. Harhoff I said seems to me that Judge Orie, that we are being punished now for the failure to reach the agreed and Mr. Harhoff agreed that we were being punished. Now, we, Mr. Krajisnik, you were being punished. I'm' just your counsel. It made it very hard work for us, but we did conscientiously try, but what I do think in this trial. I think it affected the dynamics significantly and it's referred to in one of these documents. I'm not used to being trusted by the Trial Chamber. I'm used to in 30-odd years to be completely trusted by Judges. They may think I'm incompetent, they may think I've got things, but I'm used to having my word accepted; and I'm used to it being understood that when I say I've done my best, I have done my best. That was not accepted. That was not believed by Judge Orie. It was quite clear that that was never accepted again, so we moved to this full-on mode in the trial. We abandoned not completely forever but we abandoned the negotiation mode. We had to launch that motion immediately for an application for adjournment. Didn't get us very far, did it? Let's look at -- let's look at what we might or might not have achieved by applications, it got us nowhere nor did the next one; and this team then quickly, the Defence team quickly became exhausted and when we reconvened after the recess I'm afraid this team as a whole did not have the resources and the capacity and the energy to cope with the timetable and we were -- I'm going to make this the end of my answer now, we were saved paradoxically immediately in the short term by Judge El Mahdi leaving the case. If Judge El Mahdi had not left the case when he did in December, the Defence team would not have made it through to Christmas. There would have been a physical collapse of the Defence team. We were saved from that physical collapse by that accident that Judge El Mahdi leaving the case and being replaced then by Judge Hanoteau. Judge Hanoteau of course we were going to restart when Judge Hanoteau certified that he read the papers. The extraordinary thing about that being that the date when we were going to reconvene for the trial was given to us before they even knew which Judge had been appointed to replace Judge El Mahdi and struck us as extraordinary that we were told when the trial restart, when the un-known Judge had not yet been assigned was certified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, with full respect I would like to ask you since we don't have enough time thank you very much for your answer which was really comprehensive; and I'm sure quite useful now I would like to ask you a couple of questions on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney would like to put a question on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, both appellant and the amicus allege that both as a former counsel you provided ineffective assistance during the pre-trial and trial period resulting in a denial of the appellant's right to fair trial or alternatively rendering the judgement unreliable. In the light of the event, if we want to classify it, the assistance that you received, how do you qualify it better assistance? For example, excellent treatment, special treatment ordinary fair treatment, or better than average? Would you please give me your preference if possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I -- it's me I am sure. I'd just like to be clear. Are you asking me to classify the Trial Chamber's treatment of us in relation to right to a fair trial, or are you asking me to assess my own effectiveness as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel or both? I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm just not clear enough about the question. It's obviously important, and I will answer it, by just want to be very clear what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a scale -- the Trial Chamber's -- what the Trial Chamber offered to Mr. Krajisnik by way of a fair trial on a scale of 1 to 10, 1 being completely shocking show trial, et cetera, et cetera, verdict arranged in advance to 10 being impeccable, wonderful, absolutely unsullied, immaculate fairness, 3 or 4. The second question others to judge, Your Honours. I did my best, and I believe I did my professional best in what actually turned out to be rather more difficult circumstances than I could have ever anticipated, Your Honour, but I'm not the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me remind you of some of your motions or submissions that are quoted in the transcript, and I will quote from one of them. You addressed -- in fact, it's from the trial transcript of the 26th of November, 2004 at pages 8907, 8910. You said that you felt unhappy, that you were ashamed because you were unable to go through all the materials. On the 28th of February, 2005, at 95989599 of the transcript, you say hundreds of documents are disorganised material and additionally there are dozens and dozens and dozens and dozens of thousands of pages of documents that I have not read for the most part. I don't even know what they're all about. If I open a CD, I see thousands of files, and there's no way I can find my way around them. It is absolutely impossible. This is a hopeless situation. On the 28th of September, 2005, at 17167 you state, "We have been struggling to get the minimum done." And now what I would really like to stress, on the 27th of October, 2005, at 17883 and 17884, you say the following in court: "I have constantly been raising these issues, and the Trial Chamber have been ignoring them as if this is not part of the real world. You are not interested in the things that affect the Defence in the proper way and this has been your position throughout this trial. As a result --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can you come to the question you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My question is in the course of 2004 and 2005, did you have enough time to prepare proper defence?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We were always just running to try to -- what's the metaphor? We were running to try to stay standing, really, in a way. That was -- that was what it was. I -- I -- we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you give us your evaluation of your methods of preparation? Were you able to prepare properly, because on more than one occasion you publicly addressed the Trial Chamber saying that you were short of time, that you had voluminous material, and that you were not prepared properly.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what we did is what I think any competent counsel would do, and Ms. Loukas's approach would be the same as mine. You -- you focus on what you most want to get out of cross-examination. You try to hit the key points. And you build the detail around it. Now of course you may also work the other way around and sometimes if you've got lots and lots of time and you can review all the material the process is not simply one way as I describe; but in many instances, Mr. Krajisnik, I'll be frank about it and Your Honours we didn't feel severely handicapped in relation to every single witness, sometimes it would have been very clear in relation to a particular witness what we were trying to achieve. We might have simply been trying to demonstrate that actually when you probe that witness he or she didn't really know that much directly, and you might have been able to do that actually without an enormous quantity of material, but the problem really is that you want your team anyway with appropriate delegation, you want to feel confident that your team has the time and the resources to at least review the material to make sure that you're not missing something; and that was what we were never able to do because we simply didn't have enough time and resources to deal with the volume of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. There's an important question that arises here, and it's the relationship between Krajisnik and the direct perpetrators of the crimes. I will read to you an address to the Trial Chamber on the 28th of February, 2005, by Ms. Loukas. That's on page 9577 of the transcript. She says: "The fact that we have not thoroughly read and analysed all the potentially relevant documents means that our cross-examination of these witnesses during the Prosecution case has been obstructed or prevented." These words were uttered in public by Madam Loukas before the Court. Do you agree with them?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do, though it wasn't in relation to the -- on the whole, Mr. Krajisnik, it wasn't in relation to the direct perpetrators of the crimes, by which of course you mean the crimes as we say on the ground, the specific individual perpetrators of the actual direct crimes. It wasn't really in relation to evidence of that sort that our primary problems lay. After all, Mr. Krajisnik, and we're not -- we're not breaching any privilege here, that wasn't the key to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I only asked whether you agreed with her opinion, and I'm saying that witnesses were being examined who spoke of the links between Krajisnik and the people who executed the crimes. Do you agree with her assessment? Is her answer yes? Can I take it to be yes?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think it's clear that so far as what Ms. Loukas is saying there is applicable to witnesses in that category. I whole-heartedly agree with her. I don't really disagree with her generally. I'm just saying that as a -- applying what see says there as a difficulty in relation to pure if that's not the wrong word, but the simple crime perpetrators, the on-the-ground crimes that that wasn't the main difficulty so it's -- yes, it's -- it's true what she says, but it just wasn't that -- the key problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I have to warn you, your time expired five-minutes ago. I decided to let you go on a bit farther because of the numerous questions that were put by Judges, but now I would ask you in five minutes to conclude your examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'll put a question to you which refers to the transcript of the 23rd of February, 2006. That's page 2853 and 2854. It refers expert witnesses. You said: "We had a huge deficit of time. We had insufficient time to do work which demands hours and hours, so we reached one of the most robust decisions we made, that is, we decided to stop all further investigations as regards expert testimony. So we simply removed them from the list. That's deeply regrettable. Your Honours, they were deliberately taken off the list because quite honestly we were unable to work on that issue." Could you please explain whether you agree with the decision you made then and the way in which you decided not to call experts?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, it's -- if that answer were taken as implying that we did not at some suitable stage seriously examine the question of expert witnesses, that isn't so. Ms. Loukas, under my direction and with my pretty active involvement, did a comprehensive memorandum on expert witnesses which went through three stages. It -- it marked three as we called it was very significant improvement on marks one and two; and she and I did discuss under each topic heading and in relation to the areas of expertise of the Prosecution, we did -- we did discuss it. We came to a reasonably firm provisional conclusion that actually there was very limited potential, real usefulness of expert witnesses on your side of the case, Mr. Krajisnik. That -- that was my judgement. It actually -- I must say, Your Honours, it remains my judgement, actually. The -- Ms. Loukas felt uncomfortable not being able to do more detailed work on the memorandum which she'd already done. The mark 1 and 2 were nothing fantastic, I must say; but mark 3 was a good, useful piece of work. I don't wish to exaggerate that. It was an example of -- it was a robust decision. Ideally we would have spent time on it, but actually in judging what were going to be the likely benefit to your case, it was actually a candidate for jettisoning among the priorities of work but, Your Honours, and, Mr. Krajisnik, please don't think that actually considerable thought and discussion did go into the question of expert evidence because it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put two more questions, Your Honours, brief ones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If they are very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Stewart, is the following: There were investigators at Pale, and on page 4476 of the transcript you talk about the management of the team at Pale and the organisation of their work, which was a serious issue. There was no time to give them proper instructions and to control them properly. If we asked for reports from them, there was insufficient time to study the reports. Very briefly, was this opinion correct and do you abide by it now? Just say yes or no, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My next question is the following: In the judgement there is reference to 555 -- or, rather, 555 footnotes of the judgement referred to Prosecution experts. The Prosecution called 22 experts. Can you explain to Their Honours would it have been useful for us to have called a certain number of experts to respond to this vast amount of material to which the Chamber referred when writing the judgement? Out of a thousand or so or 2.000 footnotes, 555 refer to experts.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I still don't think that expert evidence would have made any significant difference to -- on your side of the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And just one more question to round off. Can you tell Their Honours whether you as counsel can say what sort of document minutes of the Presidency are? Is it a legal document? Are these notes or what sort of document is it? Minutes -- minutes from a Presidency session, what category of document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That's not a proper question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't hear what the Prosecutor said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm objecting to the question because it's an improper question. It's calling for an opinion of this witness on something that has been specifically decided by the Trial Chamber. It was within the purview of the Trial Chamber to make this decision and not an opinion for your counsel to give today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may explain, if I may clarify. I would like to hear Counsel Stewart's reply in order to find out how he treated these minutes during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, am I to answer the question or not? It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's a completely different question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I don't quite see a different question. Could I be clear what the -- what the new version of the question now is then, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you put it again, the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you had in your possession minutes of the Presidency. Please tell us as a lawyer and as counsel what your attitude to these minutes was. What did they represent, in your view? Were they legal documents, notes, or some other type of document? How did you view them in the course of the trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Again, I don't believe it's correct, Mr. Krajisnik, your question. You're just putting it another way, but it's not really different. You simply can't put it, and that's it. The witness will not answer to your question. Mr. Krajisnik, you -- you took five more minutes beyond the minutes I gave you, so I think you should conclude now your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I rephrase the question or should I end with my examination-in-chief, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I think you should end with the examination-in-chief. You rephrased it only once more, and it was the same question actually. I think you should stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, this concludes the examination-in-chief. We will now break until 4.30, and we will continue with the amicus if he wants to take the floor for examination for 30 minutes. The meeting is adjourned for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, and I understand Judge Shahabuddeen wants to put a question now. Please. I'm sorry. Let's wait for the witness. I'm sorry, I didn't look properly around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I was quite impressed by your manner of giving testimony. Let me put this to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- we may have to make an assessment on the way Judge Orie's Trial Chamber acted, but your testimony is not really directed to any allegations against him. I apprehend that your testimony is directed at the question whether you as counsel provided effective assistance to the appellant. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose -- sorry, on the last point I'm not absolutely sure, Your Honour -- well, my testimony is directed towards answering the questions I'm asked. I rather understood Mr. Krajisnik's questions to be going primarily to the question of the fairness of the trial and the way the Trial Chamber dealt with it. Well, Your Honours, whatever the way the questions are going to I do my best to answer them but so far as what Your Honour says about Judge Orie is concerned, yes, of course, Your Honours, I don't have a brief; but it's not my brief to make allegations against anybody. Your Honours do see in the written material that I have confirmed and my facts set out there which I confirm are true that I -- it's clear that there are certain aspects of the handling of this whole matter of which I -- well, I don't show it from saying I am as counsel -- former counsel of Mr. Krajisnik rather critical. I don't shrink from that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You appreciate that the interest of this Appeals Chamber in your testimony is whether the testimony assists the Appeals Chamber in determining whether you rendered effective assistance as counsel to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly understand that to be at least one of the very important aspects. Yes, of course, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think the most important aspect, you take it from me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I was going to say, the judgement as to what's the most important aspect is a judgement for Your Honours and not for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have said somewhere that you were confronted with tens and tens and tens and tens of thousands of pages of written material. Elsewhere I think there was a reference to 500.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that this morning, and I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This afternoon, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I applaud your general proposition to the effect that it was for you to form an intelligent appreciation of the substance of the case and to proceed that way, delegating as you thought proper to members of your team. By the way, the Tribunal supplied you with funds to enable you to employ both yourself and co-counsel and some assistance. How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How much funds or how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's -- in the -- at the beginning of the trial, from what I recall now, there was myself. There was Chris Lukic as my co-counsel, Tatjana Cmeric as my case manager, a young woman called Lucy Robb who was a recently but extremely intelligent graduate from Australia as a legal assistant. I think we had maybe one other legal assistant at that time or perhaps a little while afterwards, and then another one in the summer. It wasn't a big team. There was the -- the maximum number -- I'm not even sure it was that, but the Registry has all this information. At the most -- it was the core three were myself, Ms. Loukas, and Ms. Cmeric, and we had one or two other legal assistants at that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. All right. And you were able with that assistance to manage the proceedings, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the way that I've described, Your Honour, barely. And -- and that was true throughout. I think the description I use was of running just to stay standing, and that really was the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as the funding was concerned, it was -- that was -- that was difficult, because it is an aspect of this case. The Registry provides, and Your Honours will be familiar with this, the Registry provides a designated amount for -- this of course was a category 3 case, but assesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's the highest category.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the highest category, of course, but I think the general feeling I don't think was controversial was even among category 3 cases this was pretty high up the scale, but Registry provides a standard amount; but it also assesses what contribution to that sum the accused should make and the Registry only ever provides the net amount -- I've got to say this was -- it was a bone of contention between Mr. Krajisnik and me pretty much throughout the entire case. We -- we were only paid the net amount, of course, and we only had the net amount until very late in the trial when the Registry did provide some extra funding towards the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- if I may proceed to say this: That the Trial Chamber, this I gather from you, did not hold hearings on every week of the working day, three times per week, and in addition it gave certain adjournments, and that was a pattern which enabled you to manage the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That isn't -- that's not -- that's not quite how it happened, Your Honour. The -- clearly the actual dates of hearings can be seen from the record. For the first few months of the trial up to July, yes, it was -- it was patchy in various ways that one sees. There was that start that I referred to, and then we resumed after April. There was an adjournment in May. I forget precisely why there. Then there was the agreed facts exercise which was ultimately aborted. But after that when we resumed in the autumn but not every week because it depended on what happened with witnesses and so on, but in principle we were sitting five days a week. That was the scheduled contemplated trial pattern, yes. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you sit every day in the week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I -- it -- it felt like it but that doesn't mean it did. The -- we certainly did not have -- it's not like, for example, my current trial. We certainly didn't have a designated day a week off. And this was actually when I first agreed to come into the case it was understood that there would be a regular pattern of -- this is what I was told what would happen of a week a month or a day each week off. It wasn't like that. The basic -- once the trial really got under way according to a more rigorous schedule after the summer recess in 2004, I think the basic principle was it was five days a week. There was no designated day a week off. But how that works out in practice Your Honours will know. Of course it's in the vagaries of trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me get on to another point if I may. You remember that on 28th of February, 2005, the Trial Chamber gave its reasons relating to the six months adjournment when it said there: "I have to say that --" that is Mr. Stewart -- Mr. Krajisnik said, Mr. Krajisnik said to the Trial Chamber: "I have to say that whatever both my counsels stated here today I endorse. I do not have anything to comment, to raise in relation to the services provided by my counsel. They are both very good lawyers." Do you remember hearing those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't remember it was on the 28th of February, Your Honour, but I -- of course I distinctly remember a number of occasions when Mr. Krajisnik said -- said something complimentary about us, yes, do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember that on the 18th of August, 2005, the Trial Chamber gave its reasons for oral decision on the appellant's claim to self-representation? In paragraph 35 it said that: "The Defence team," including yourself, "that this is not a case of an existing dysfunctional Defence team or of a complete breakdown in the client/attorney relationship. On the contrary. The current Defence team is competent, dedicated, functioning, and working well with the accused. There is no public interest in dismantling such a team." That was said by the Trial Chamber in denying the appellant's claim to self-representation. Do you remember those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do broadly remember them, Your Honour, yes. I -- yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are they substantially reflective of the position do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour. I -- I believe they are with this qualification that -- well, "dysfunctional" is a quite strong word sometimes. There were by that time -- the stresses and strains of the case were certainly causing far more difficulty than might have been apparent to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Stewart, I'd like to put a question to you. You mentioned earlier fairly extensively the difficulties you had with the funds allotted to you and the lack of time.
