You also added, however, that you were saved - I think that was the word you used - by the departure Judge El Mahdi leaving the case, and you were therefore saved by the fact that it took some time for Judge Hanoteau, who was going to be replacing him, to read all the papers and catch up on the case. Can we assume that this lack of time was made up for in those circumstances in that from that time onwards you were more comfortable in defending your client Mr. Krajisnik? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly helpful, Your Honour. There's no question about that. That much time was available for us. But it wouldn't be -- it wouldn't be true to say that it in anywhere near enabled us to make up the entire deficit. It didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it wasn't the entire deficit, can you maybe give us an assessment of how much of that deficit was made up for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Judge -- Judge El Mahdi left the case -- 14th of December comes into my head, but I don't know whether it was. But it was sometime in December, and so we had two and a half months. Ms. Loukas, as I remember, went to Australia for about a month over that recess which she needed to do. There was no question about that. I absolutely endorsed and encouraged that, and she went not -- not working on the case. So there was the recess, and I worked, I think, quite a bit of the recess myself. So when we came back from the recess in January there were then six weeks. I don't think that a lot of catching could have been done until early or mid-January when we were all back here, and then we had those -- we had those six weeks. Your Honour, I'm sorry, it's not intended at all to be an unhelpful answer if I say we just had six weeks. So, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, and thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you spoke of the tactic or strategy of the Trial Court to allow fairly extensive adjournments so that you could come up to speed with reading and preparing for the trial. Was there any time during the case that you feel you came entirely up to speed and you reached adequate command of the material? This is my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't, Your Honour. When you say I spoke of the tactical strategy of the Trial Court to allow fairly extensive adjournments, I am -- I'm recognising that in the earlier months of the trial, from the 4th or whatever it was, of February through to June and then including that agreed facts exercise, I'm recognising that -- that the number of sitting days in relation to the number of available sitting days was not that massive. So, yes, there was -- there was a degree of flexibility, no question about it. So later on not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you have never come completely up to speed and being in command of the material that you would have wanted professionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is my view, Your Honour, but critically we certainly were never in that position by the time the Prosecution case had closed. I don't mean that we were fully later, but -- but critically in dealing with the Prosecution case, no, we never felt comfortable about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. My second question is this: Responding to Judge Guney earlier today, I believe you gave three to four points to the trial's fairness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you point to something specific that you could have done but did not do because you did not have enough time to prepare and which may have caused real prejudice to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, first of all it's, if you like, I'm afraid the rather general point I'll be making that we had, in relation to the case generally and specifically in cross-examination the Prosecution witnesses we felt that we never had the time or the resources to be confident that we had examined all the material which might have been helpful. Now, the next stage, what material that was and if we had had it what we would have been able to do with it, that's -- that's I've got to say from where I sit that's a bit speculative by definition because that's exactly what I don't know. Another thing I will say also that the 60 per cent guideline that the Trial Chamber adopted in the time it allowed for cross-examination was in my view and consistent view; and we made representations very often to that effect, far too rigidly applied. We had a rather -- a continual run-in. Judge Orie would keep referring to it as the 60 per cent rule, and I would keep correcting him by reminding him it was a guideline and he would say, "Yes I agree," and then two minutes later he would refer to it as a rule and that was each of us really trying to put our position. It was to a considerable extent applied as a rule, and I can't remember them, Your Honour, but on the transcript there will be I think a number of occasions when I protested that -- that I did have more cross-examination and I was being chopped off, and we sometimes came in under the figure. So -- so that is one specific illustration. And that is directly relevant. After all, if we did have cross-examination that we'd identified and wanted to put, we felt that was unduly rigid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The question of your being cut off in cross-examination is to my mind different from the question whether you had enough time to come to grips with the material --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completely agree, Your Honour. I completely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was really trying to answer Judge Meron's question with two separate examples. Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You spoke in this connection of tens and tens and tens and tens of thousands of pages. May I ask you this question: If you personally had to read each of these pages and to linger over any associated photographs, would you be in a position to commence the trial as of this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- Your Honour's really anticipated my answer because my answer would be I would still be down there in the office reading them. Yes, Your Honour, is spot on with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Before -- before giving the floor to the amicus, I got -- did I get it correctly that you said that the -- there was a break in the trial when Judge El Mahdi left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I forget the precise date, but I think it was the 14th or around the middle of December. It was shortly before the recess, the winter recess in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I didn't check in the records of any minutes, but it must have been one month earlier than.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Than ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Than your recollection. It must have been mid-November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected, Your Honour. My recollected is because I thought we cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... elected as judge by the General Assembly that must have been the term expired on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you had another four weeks more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: No, I'm just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just invite the Trial Chamber to check that specific date because it could easily be because it could easily be that there was a time lag between Judge El Mahdi not being re-elected and deciding he would leave the case but, Your Honour, it's eminently checkable and, you know, I'm not -- I'm not going to say I know, it's just easily checkable, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure. Sure. Well, let's move on to the -- to the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I just want to ask you at the time to begin with at the time you undertook the defence of Mr. Krajisnik you had 33 years experience as a barrister?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'd been called to the bar 33 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Whereas 18 years were as Queen's Counsel?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Seventeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Seventeen?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your practice was mainly in transferring and commercial work?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you had some experience of crime?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I had experience of crime and also I had experience of sort of quasi-crime if you like of hearings before the European Court of Human Rights of which I had been involved down in Turkey, fact-finding hearings by committees of the Strasbourg court into cases against Turkey which clearly involve criminal allegations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You had sufficient experience of criminal work to know that pre-trial preparation of a defence is absolutely essential?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It's rather essential in civil cases as well, Mr. Nicholls, as well, so yes, of course I was very well aware of that. That applies generally to -- to any case for any client, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this case when you took it on, there was for practical purposes, so far as you were concerned, practically no pre-trial preparation?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: You mean as it turned out when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As it turned out?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: You're talking about what I took over from -- you're not talking about our team's preparation, but you're talking about what I took over from the previous team are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What you took over from the previous team.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: There wasn't -- there wasn't very much evidence of readiness for trial. I don't believe -- put it this way bluntly, and I could elaborate a bit, I do not believe that at the time that Mr. Brashich was taken off the case around April 2004, I do not believe that he was prepared to start the trial and could have started the trial effectively on May the 14th if he had been lucky enough not to have been suspended by the New York Bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it right that he provided you with practically no work product?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that he at an earlier hearing had said to Judge Orie when he was asked for his work product that it was all in his head?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's true, and I wish that in my initial discussions with the Registry I wish that somebody had drawn that statement to my attention earlier, because I wasn't aware of it until a while later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You didn't get a complete or reasonably full set of papers until sometime towards the end of November of 2003; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't get what you might call Brashich-style full set of papers until that date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it was then that you and Ms. Loukas were able to have serious discussions about the situation that you were faced with?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's true. Added to the fact -- added the fact that the Registry actually wouldn't pay to bring Ms. Loukas here until -- I don't know whether it was one month before the trial or six weeks before the trial. She was in Australia. They weren't prepared to bring her here anyway -- they brought her here once for a short visit in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas was an experience the counsel in criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: She was, yes. She worked for the public defender's office. I think she had for all or most of her career she worked for the public defender's office in Sydney, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did she indicate to you that it would take at least a year to prepare this case properly?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember it but I'm not -- I wouldn't be surprised if she said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did she during the months of December, January 2003 to 2004, did she constantly urge you to make an application for an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, she did, yes, and she -- and she said we must go on strike. We must refuse to start the trial. She said a large number of things she felt very strongly about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In spite of that you took the view that the case should be -- proceed on the basis that you've told us in your evidence in answer to questions from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't take the view the case should proceed, Mr. Nicholls. I took the realistic view that it clearly was going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: And it was not my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were prepared not to make an application for adjournment on the basis that you didn't think it would succeed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I was prepared not to make -- as I explained I was prepared not to make an application for adjournment because I made the most vigorous representations and Ms. Loukas was with me at a many of these meetings. I made the most vigorous representations to the Trial Chamber because in this -- I soon discovered that in this institution far more than the courts that you and I are used to routinely; and I don't mean this in itself critically, it can have its negative aspects, but I soon discovered that far more of this sort of thing gets discussed and dealt with outside the formal court environment than a you or I would be used to in our own jurisdiction and I decided to -- we were doing it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that had you made an application for an adjournment there was at least a possibility that it might have been granted by three Judges?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't actually, Mr. Nicholls. I think it was practically doomed to failure I do because they -- they would have been dealing with an application where they would say, Well we're only asking you to do 18 days and we've given you a flexible schedule over the next couple of months. Ask for an adjournment in a couple of months' time if that doesn't work, which was a master of fact Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: What I had in mind was that -- excuse me, if you would just let me finish my answer. The question of whether and when to time an application for adjournment was under constant discussion; and for the reasons that I've described we gave up on this negotiation mode which actually when you look at the -- at the trial schedule from February to end of June was moderately successful, actually, in getting us some time during that period but when it call broke down, the collapse of the agreed facts exercise, we did then make that application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that by not making an application to the Trial Chamber you at least lost the opportunity of making a further appeal to the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. Nicholls, because I am -- my judgement at the time and I actually still think -- I don't think I was wrong. My judgement at the time was that an application would have failed, and Mr. Nicholls retrospectively I mean getting a bit hypothetical, it follows my judgement that if that application had failed we would have stood any realistic chance of success on appeal is that no we wouldn't; and we didn't appeal maybe you're coming to that. I don't know. We didn't appeal the refusal for the first application for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with hindsight that your decision was wrong?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall saying on one occasion, "I shouldn't have underestimated the problem for so long. I shouldn't have just brushed aside certain matters. I should have brought this to the attention of the Trial Chamber a long time ago"? That's the July application --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember that perfectly well, Mr. Nicholls. If you say do I agree with the benefit of hindsight that my decision was wrong with the benefit of hindsight we ended up no better offer than if I had made the application at the beginning but that's not quite the same thing. If you're asking me now do I think, do I think that when I made that judgement in February or just in the run-up to February it was a wrong judgement at the time, no, I don't think it was and I would like to say in relation to those comments which you -- you quote from the transcript there is an element, and I don't think I was misleading anybody here, there was an element there of wanting to mollify and boost the morale of my extremely beleaguered team, and particularly Ms. Loukas. And I wasn't saying and the discussions with Ms. Loukas didn't involve self-flagellation on my part and I got it all wrong, Chrissa, and it was a complete blunder on my part. It wasn't that, but I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: But I -- Mr. Nicholls, I wanted to acknowledge that as it had turned out we were still beleaguered and actually another, if you like, disagreement between us was with the benefit of hindsight I was too trusting; and I did acknowledge this to Ms. Loukas I was too trusting of the Trial Chamber's willingness to look as we went along at future applications for an adjournment situation as it developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may stop you for a moment if you understand. I've only got half an hour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please refrain from overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've only half an hour in which to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Nicholls, but I wish to answer your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just follow on for a moment, please I just want to consider the result of the decision. You started the trial on the 3rd of February of --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I still don't know whether the 3rd or the 4th but it was a Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's accept whatever it was. At the second application for adjournment you said that your team had only read 15 per cent of the papers in the trial.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Did I say that my not quibbling, did I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please don't interrupt the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Otherwise the interpreters cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, of course I accept that point completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me put the question again.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the second application for adjournment that is 13 months into the trial, you said your team had only read 15 per cent of the papers. Would you care to answer what percentage of the papers your team had read on the 3rd, 4th of February when the trial began?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nicholls speak more into the microphone for the interpreters, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1 per cent, 2 per cent. I don't -- Mr. Nicholls, if there were half a million papers we must have read a few thousand, I suppose, so it's a small percentage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you consider it was proper to commence a trial when your team had only read between 1 and 2 per cent of the papers?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't think it was a good idea, Mr. Nicholls, but proper -- if I may answer your question, to some extent this was if you like a particular discussion between Chrissa Loukas and me. She said we must go on strike and I said actually, Chrissa, if we are in court and if the Court says the trial starts, we may not like it, we have protested it, we may fight it; but in the end if they say the trial starts, the trial starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go to the next question, please. At that time, the 3rd or 4th of February had you properly your team properly conducted any investigations into the credibility of the Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We hadn't been able to conduct any investigations, Mr. Nicholls, because the idea Ms. Cmeric, Ms. Loukas, and I, we'd not been able to go anywhere else. We'd not been able to go down to the region. We had the people in Pale. To that degree, the people in Pale supplied us the information from time to time, but I think I just have to say with all honesty, Mr. Krajisnik probably won't like me saying it, they were amateurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me leave that aside. Had you examined the Prosecution's material?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: As much as we could, yes. We examined the Prosecution in relation to the witnesses that were coming up, Mr. Nicholls, particularly to whom of course we gave priority. We examined as much as possible of the Prosecution material and Ms. Cmeric was helpful; Ms. Cmeric is a highly intelligent, able woman who had had some previous involvement in the case and did have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Had you examined any Defence material that might be available?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Relatively little. Ms. Cmeric, actually, as I remember, I couldn't be absolutely sure of timing on this, Mr. Nicholls, but because a lot of that even most of it if you like was in B/C/S, Ms. Cmeric did look at that sort of material she -- she was pretty dismissive of a lot of it actually she --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have a proof of evidence from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No we didn't, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Had you taken any detailed instructions from him for the purposes of cross-examination and for his defence?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To what extent?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we concentrated in the circumstances, we concentrated particularly on the witnesses that were coming up that was the -- that was the natural focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the proof what proof of evidence did you have?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We didn't have a proof. There was no formal proof. There was no proof of evidence prepared by my predecessor and nor did we attempt at that pre-trial stage nor did we attempt to -- to prepare a proof of Mr. Krajisnik. It wasn't that we didn't, I did prepare one eventually of course, but it wasn't at that stage a priority, Mr. Nicholls, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Had you by the 3rd or 4th of February identified any Defence witnesses apart from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I doubt it, Mr. Nicholls, sent in -- in very -- I -- I doubt it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas complained very much that there was no proper defence case strategy. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I recall Ms. Loukas complaining about that and actually quite a lot of other things a lot of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was she correct that there was no defence case strategy?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Not really. The -- the -- it was -- we -- we both agreed that we of course we would have liked more time. We would have liked more time on everything. We both agreed that we would have liked more time to develop the strategy in more detail, to move from the strategy -- well, to the sort of things you're talking about, to the strategy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I haven't finished my answer, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Remember I haven't [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I remember; but if you ask me a question, please, Your Honours, I wish to be able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you take it a little more shortly please, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: If it enables me to answer the question, Mr. Nicholls, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: As I think I indicated earlier, we were able and we had a clear enough idea of the strategy for that not to be the problem in the examination of the Prosecution witnesses that we were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the position is, is it not, that on the 3rd or 4th of February your team was grossly unprepared to commence a trial?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We'd done our best, Mr. Nicholls, but it follows that -- that it -- we -- the trial was started too early.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please the question is: On the 3rd or 4th of February, your team was grossly unprepared to commence a trial.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: If you're looking at the whole trial, yes, we were; of course we were. We knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there could be no doubt about it, that if you were to put yourself in Mr. Krajisnik's position it could not in the circumstances be a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We told Mr. Krajisnik. You're quite right. It's the only qualification was that as I've indicated I don't think we ended up particularly hampered in relation to that first batch of witnesses if February; but yes we were grossly under-prepared to start a trial, a full trial. We made that clear to Mr. Krajisnik. We regretted it. He knew we thought that. There was no disguise. We didn't want to worry him unduly for heaven's stake but he was our client. We owed it to him to give him our frank view of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that in no way there could be no fair trial in the circumstances of the 3rd of or 4th of February?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: There couldn't have been a fair trial starting on the 3rd or 4th of February unless -- unless suitable leeway were given later and suitable time were given later. It didn't follow as night follows day that starting the trial only the 4th of February meant that it was bound to be unfair, but it was going to be unfair unless adjustments, and radical adjustments were made pretty soon after that to -- to allow us adequate opportunity to -- to present Mr. Krajisnik's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas said that you needed 12 months, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We're talking -- we were never going to get 12 months, Mr. Nicholls, I mean we have to operate from that position, but if Ms. Loukas and I'd agree if you're saying well; and I would have agreed with her if you say what -- what -- what ought we to be allowed by this institution and what ought we to have been given in order to prepare for this trial in the way that she and I would both be used to, yes, I never disagreed with her about that sort of assessment and wouldn't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: At the 65 ter meeting on the 3rd of January, Judge Orie referred to the papers in the case as being in a state of chaos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is absolutely right because apart from anything else he must have got that information from me because how would he have known I had the Defence papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he acknowledged the difficulties that you had?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Nicholls, I don't know. You'd have to cite to me what constituted that acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But in spite of his saying to you that the Defence would have difficulties and that the papers were in chaos, you still did not make an application for an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I told Judge Orie there and then sitting across a table in the light of everything he was saying that the -- that that was not a suitable date on which to start the trial and Judge Orie said, "This trial will start on the --" whatever it was, the 3rd or the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You finally made your first application for an adjournment on the -- in the months of July --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct. After the breakdown of the agreed facts exercise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in that case of the adjournment you expressed all your anxieties about the time and resources that you had?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I suggest to you is that it was at that moment in time that you indicated that you shouldn't have underestimated the problem for so long and that you should have listened to your co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: The -- the last bit, Mr. Krajisnik, was to keep my team happy. I did listen to my co-counsel. Of course I did. I just didn't agree with her all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that application for an adjournment in July 2004 failed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you didn't apply -- you didn't appeal --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the decision --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- not granting you the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Because I was about as sure as I could be that we would lose, and I thought what would happen is what did in fact happen with the second application for an adjournment, which we did appeal. I thought that the severe danger of appealing was that there would be some possibly ringing endorsement from the Appeals Chamber but that the appeal would fail and that would actually only encourage the Trial Chamber to push the trial along. I preferred to leave it. I preferred to make a renewed application at some later date which we always felt that the point would come where we would have to make yet a further application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: So it was a judgement, Mr. Nicholls, which if you're -- maybe I'm anticipating the next question. It was a judgement which I actually think was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was it a judgement with which your client agreed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know, I simply don't remember, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you consult him?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you regard it as a proper exercise of judgement not to make an application for an adjournment or any other application on the basis that you do not think the Tribunal will grant the application?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly think it's a highly material factor, Mr. -- Mr. Nicholls, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The position was that the first and the second applications for an adjournment failed, as you have indicated, and you were left in a position where you were effectively dealing with the case as it went along adopting really a position of fighting -- fighting fires, fighting bush fires; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's entirely correct, Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is the position that in truth you never, never could make up for the lack of preparation which you'd had at the outset?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: The outset meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you started the trial.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We could -- we could never make up for -- for where we were. Yes, we could never make up for where we found ourselves when we came into the case and where we found ourselves when the trial started. I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so far as cross-examination was concerned, you were never in a position to be able to say that you were able to examine all the material that you needed to examine in order to conduct effective cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that probably wasn't in relation to every witness, Mr. Nicholls, but generally speaking and certainly when we are talking about, if you like, the more important witnesses because plainly there's such a category that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It applied in respect of certain witnesses where you felt that you did not have the material and so far as other witnesses were concerned would the position be because of not be able to look at material you'd never be in a position to know?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it's a little bit sweeping to say never because some witnesses, Mr. Nicholls, were inevitably relatively minor in the ambit of their evidence; and in fact, you could be confident for practical purposes that -- that you'd looked at what you needed to look at, yes. But that's not a very large number, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to come on to the Defence case for a moment.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were very concerned as to whether you had sufficient time to prepare the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That involved in the first case considering witnesses who would give evidence before Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Deciding who those witnesses were.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The order in which they gave their evidence, and of course its content.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. The only qualification I make about that is that the order in which they gave their evidence would be low down the list of priorities really because frankly when you get into the question of -- and the Prosecution I'm sure found this as well, when you get into the question of bringing witnesses from the region to here your order is often dictated by who you can actually get here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient time to prepare the examination at those -- one, to decide who the witnesses were; two, to prepare what they were going to say?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I've got to say in relation to the Defence case, Mr. Nicholls, it wasn't as -- the position wasn't as dire really as it had been in dealing with the Prosecution case. We never -- we never had as much time as we would have wanted, and we had enormous difficulty at the early stage of putting together and filing that list; and we can see from the record the enormous problems in meeting the trial's -- Trial Chamber's deadlines before we started the Defence case. Once we were into it, it wasn't -- it wasn't the most dire and difficult aspect of the case for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ask for more time?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We -- yes, we -- we -- in the -- the filing of the 65 ter list and the question of starting the Defence case, yes, we -- we asked -- I think on several occasions, we asked for more time and for deadlines to be deferred, and as far as I remember there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there considerable difficulties in providing summaries of the Defence [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there were. Let me add that, of course, we had the additional difficulty at that point that Ms. Loukas had left the case and Mr. Josse was new to the case and that was an extra difficulty we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did those difficulties cause considerable difficulties with -- problems with Judge Orie and they brought you into conflict with him?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Lots of things cause conflict with Judge Orie because we -- we didn't like the rulings that Judge Orie made, and I think -- I must say, Mr. Nicholls, I don't know, I'm not a mind-reader, but I do think that a great deal of difficulty went back to what I call that breakdown in the summer of 2004 and the agreed facts exercise, but yes it was not a happy ship although it had been for many months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, sorry. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to leave the courtroom for just a few minutes with your leave, and then I will be back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers please slow down and make pauses between questions and answers both for the sake of interpretation and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, noted. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We can resume. Mr. Nicholls, you still have three minutes to conclude your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, did you consider that you had sufficient time for the preparation of the final brief?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, not really. It was terribly tight. It was incredibly hard work, yes, but you expect hard work. We would have liked quite a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the course of the trial, is it right that you were very much concerned with priorities?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's not unusual, but yes, we were very much concerned with priorities, Mr. Nicholls. That's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But particularly so in this case because of the time that was available to conduct the work that had to be done?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I hundred per cent agree with that, Mr. Nicholls, yes. That's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did that include cutting down on legal research?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, it did, but I -- that -- again that -- that was not actually really that much of a problem. We -- yes, we would have liked to do more. You know, sometimes -- sometimes counsel just want a break. Ms. Loukas, I think, would have dearly loved to occasionally be released from the grind of cross-examining and do some legal research; and I respected that feeling, but we were not hampered in the sense that we did enough -- enough, Mr. Nicholls, to -- to know where we were going. I mean, we -- we needed a legal road map, if you like of where we were you go we did that. And yes, we did enough to do that, yes. It would be -- a high priority to know at lease where you're going legally, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First you had to identify the members of the team who were to do the research?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That wasn't all that difficult, Mr. Nicholls, given the members of the team. There weren't all that many choices. Actually, I selected myself, actually, quite often for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Secondly, so far as any particular exercise was concerned, you need to identify the people who were to do it.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your team was very small indeed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so far as the lawyers were concerned, there was to begin with yourself and Chrissa Loukas?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then later you and Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Josse.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Commonly known as Josse, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were they really the two of them or the two of you as it might be, were you really able to cope in the time that you had with the identification of topics, the investigation of the of the topics as you required as you would do to provide a quality service to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nicholls I'd also like to add, you said there's only counsel; for example, the person I mentioned, Lucy Robb, who was a legal assistant came with glowing prizes and honours from law school in Australia. It is not as if we had no legal resources. But the answer quality service, legal research is not a problem, actually, ultimately. I'm repeating myself really , Mr. Nicholls. We were able to know enough about where we were going legally, we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I have to say that your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then I stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to the Prosecution to -- for the cross-examination of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I gather from your testimony in response the questions of Mr. Nicholls that Mr. Krajisnik was very active in his defence?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He -- he -- Mr. Krajisnik is -- is very hard working, and he produced large quantities of material, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you during the course of his defence meet with him on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: With respect to the Prosecution case, did Mr. Krajisnik provide you with are proposed questions to ask to each of the Prosecution witnesses that testified?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I don't know whether he always presented his material in the form of questions or sometimes in the -- in the form of notes, but one way or another I think he always, and I think always, produced notes in his own language which then so Tatjana Cmeric would usually be the first point at which that would be considered, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And with respect to documents, the half million pages of documents that had been provided by the Prosecution as disclosure, had a copy of those documents been made available to Mr. Krajisnik from the beginning of the disclosure and throughout its -- throughout the pre-trial phase and during the trial phase?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I -- that wasn't really feasible. The -- certainly not in hard copy. There was no question of -- there was no question of duplicating the -- the room full of stuff that we had down at our office, but he was provided with -- we -- we had a very regular exchange of CDs with Mr. Krajisnik by which, of course, he was supplied with material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And is it fair to say that Mr. Krajisnik's input into the case was very strong and because of his knowledge of the political history and -- and having lived the political history of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik -- yes, of course Mr. Krajisnik knew a great deal about the -- about his own case, and he is extremely industrious and after all had an incentive; but he is by nature very industrious, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you use your professional judgement in determining whether and how to put Mr. Krajisnik's questions to the various witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we -- we did our best to sift the material that came from Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik is a demanding client but I don't blame him in the least for that. I'd rather have a client who gives you input than one that doesn't. He provided us with material which was with the other material demanding to sift and consider, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. Now, during the course of the Prosecution's case, am I correct that for the municipality witnesses you received a binder that included all of the material that the Prosecution intended to lead in respect of the municipalities in advance of the municipality evidence that would be called during the course of the case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not at all sure that -- that consistently that material was provided in advance of the evidence in relation to that municipality. I -- I just don't recall. I've -- I have a feeling it may not have been, but that's -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you not also receive a binder of the proposed evidence of the witness, all previous statements of the witness, and any documents to which the witness might refer during the course of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we had had that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you at least knew for the purposes of preparation what case -- what evidence the Prosecution intended to draw from the witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, because in -- as you quite rightly indicate, we -- the statements, I think it must have been -- well, not just rare, but I don't suppose it happened or if it did on one or two rare occasions there was not a statement of the witness indicating what he was going to say apart from the 65 ter summaries of course which were -- with respect were pretty variable on the Prosecution's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, let's back up a moment. Let's go to when you were first retained as counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. Did you meet with Mr. Krajisnik on occasion prior to the commencement of the trial?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you receive from him instructions as to what his defence would be?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And when you commenced as counsel there was already a pre-trial brief prepared by the Brashich team which by my reading basically put the Prosecution to the test of proving its case with no concessions or admissions by the Defence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you receive any instructions from Mr. Krajisnik to take another position, a more conciliatory position during the course of the presentation of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I don't recall whether it was with what degree of reluctance, I don't know, but Mr. Krajisnik accepted our going into the agreed facts exercise and attempt which was -- which was a very different approach from Mr. Brashich, who I believe from talking to him what I seen would -- would not contemplate that sort of process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: When you backed away from the admitted facts process prior to communicating --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Agreed facts. I'm sorry. Agreed facts process. Did you consult with Mr. Krajisnik on the decision that you were proposing to take?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, I think that -- I think that the particular decision to pull the plug, as I put it, on that was taken by me over a weekend without final consultation with Mr. Krajisnik, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And when you advised Mr. Krajisnik did he encourage you to recommence the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Krajisnik certainly didn't have any problem with that. After all, if I'd expected he'd have any problem with my decision I would have left it to go and see him at the Detention Unit. No. There was no -- there was no difficulty about that decision. In fact, my team were delighted with that decision. I was, if you like, the last one to want to keep trying on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about your understanding of the defence of Mr. Krajisnik when the trial started. You mentioned that you had spoken on many occasions to Mr. Krajisnik before the commencement of the Prosecution case. Did you have a specific understanding of what the basic defence strategy was when you cross-examined the first Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you that the Defence strategy can be summarised as follows: One, that you wanted to put as much distance between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That was certainly included in it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Number two was to show that Mr. Krajisnik was merely the president of the Assembly, a politician, and not someone who was in a decision-making role or capacity.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- it's a little bit more -- I don't blame you, but it's a little bit more crudely put than I would have formulated it, but very broadly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That there was no link between Mr. Krajisnik and the crimes that were committed on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Links were the key, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That he was not a member of the expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and that -- that's -- THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise. I don't know whether the Prosecutor should continue to put such leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't believe these are leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: They're leading questions, but I'm entitled to put them, Your Honour. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] If he does have that right, I apologise; but I believe the Prosecutor should rely on the examination-in-chief and put less leading questions, because he has a professional lawyer before him; so he will answer in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't believe these are leading questions. Whether they're restricted or not to the cross-examination -- to the examination-in-chief, this is something that we should appreciate later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Just to respond briefly, since we've opened up the whole area of fair trial and the effectiveness of counsel, this goes to the core of how effective counsel was at the commencement of the trial and throughout, and I will -- I won't stray from the effectiveness of counsel and the fairness of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you also, Mr. Stewart, as part of the Defence strategy, attempt to show that Mr. Krajisnik was a participant in international negotiations and looking for a peaceful solution to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, not just in the international context, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you also had as a strategic goal know that Mr. Krajisnik had no links with the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we certainly wished to minimise, show -- yes. Show how little or non-existent they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And that Variant A and B was not an official document?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we certainly wished to undermine the Prosecution's Variant A and B thesis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And also that the six strategic goals were not inherently criminal, and it was policy, not a criminal plan?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you received instructions as to what the goal was in terms of the strategic goal for the Defence from Mr. Krajisnik before starting to cross-examine the first witness in February of 2004?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: You're moving -- you're using the phrase "Strategic goal" quite separately from the six strategic goals here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, though after all, we were counsel, so the actual -- the actual strategy of running the trial was for us based on what Mr. Krajisnik instructed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, but you as counsel, based on the instructions of Mr. Krajisnik, had identified those specific goals which we had just discussed as being the principle areas that you wanted either to bring out positively or to the extent that a witness was commenting on them challenge for the purposes of setting up the Defence case that you knew would be coming; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and based on the instructions Mr. Krajisnik. After all, some of these goals were blindingly obvious without any serious need for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the Appeals Chamber can look at the opening statement, but I -- that you made to the Trial Chamber in -- I believe it's October of 2005.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But all of the goals were identified there as basically issues that the Defence had identified and was undertaking to prove, for example, that Mr. Krajisnik was a mere president of the Assembly and had no authority to make decisions in relation to the crimes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't specifically remember any more, but -- but, yes, it would surprise me if such matters were not included in the opening statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And, in fact, the Defence case that you did present was directed at establishing all of the Defence goals that had been defined before the Prosecution commenced and would do its very best to show the Trial Chamber a view that was different than presented from the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that Mr. Krajisnik had always intended to testify on his own defence.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That was absolutely clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. And it was made clear to the Chamber that he would be testifying subject to a 98 -- a favourable 92 bis decision, both by you and by Mr. Krajisnik during the course of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, and it's -- it's relatively unusual, but it was absolutely crystal clear that Mr. Krajisnik intended to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the allocation of time that was devoted to the Defence case, Mr. Krajisnik testified for 40 days, did he not, in total?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was something like that. Its is a matter of record, but yes, that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in terms of the presentation of his evidence, I think initially, in-chief it was 23 days?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Again that sounds right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And were there any areas in his examination-in-chief that you felt were not fully articulated?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't feel at the time when his examination-in-chief finished that there were any glaring gaps, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And during the decisions in -- in who would be called for the Defence was Mr. Krajisnik involved in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: When a witness was called to the stand we have it suggested by a witness previous that sometimes Mr. Krajisnik was surprised that the witness was in the witness box. Do you recall calling a witness that you had not previously discussed with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In preparing for the witnesses called in the Defence case, did you consult actively with Mr. Krajisnik and get his advice on what questions should be put to the witness and how the witness might help him in his case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that -- if -- if you means Mr. Josse and/or me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Because by that time Ms. Loukas had left the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If we could just go for a moment to closed session, please. I'm going to deal with some private or sealed documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with a few of the documents that had been tendered during the course of the 115 applications. I'm going to start with Exhibit -- I think it's AD1, which is the letter of George Mano.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I haven't got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I just --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It's my understanding that you became aware of the letter sometime in September, October of 2004.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was September, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you were allowed to provide a response --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- to the letter by Registry?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't allowed. They couldn't stop me. I can write to the Registry without their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of the letter itself, perhaps you can just give me your comment to the allegations in the letter to the extent that you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't read it for a very long time. I'll do my best to remember it. The -- there was a certain amount of general personal abuse and character assassination, as I remember; but he had some big complaint about the agreed facts process. I do remember that. I -- George Mano had no legal qualification that I remember. He had very little idea at all, but I didn't blame him for it, of what we were trying to do in a legal case. What I did blame him for was not appreciating that he had very little idea. And he and I, we never became great friends I've got to say. He was very resentful of the fact that when he asked me if I would ask the registrar if he could go and see Mr. Krajisnik on his own because, "I've got a few questions to ask Mr. Krajisnik," I said, "No I wouldn't," and he asked me, "Why not?" I said, "Because there wasn't the slightest chance that the registrar would give such permission," and I didn't want it anyway. And frankly, I regarded the idea -- he took that very badly, but I regarded the idea of an intern getting shirty with me because I wouldn't let him go and see Mr. Krajisnik on his own about something, frankly, it was fantastic. I mean, he really had a nerve. He was extremely importunate. I remember taking him along, which is -- I mean, it's something I like to do to involve interns. I took him along to a meeting with Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger, I think, was there as well and Mr. Hannis as well on agreed facts. At some point Mr. Harmon I could see was slightly stunned, was slightly stunned to have George Mano pipe up from the end of the table, "I can't accept that, Mr. Harmon." I mean, what a nerve he had. He seemed to think that what we were supposed to do was learn all about Serb history, whereas our view was we should learn enough about Serb history to be able to run the case. I could go on. I mean, that's what I seem to remember. I remember some extremely scurrilous personal stuff as well. I remember some actual factual rubbish. I remember him talking to me about going to Spain for two weeks, which I didn't go. I went with three of my children and I worked every morning until they saw fit to get up which was about lunchtime for them at that time. And I went to Croatia for a few days with my one-year-old then child which didn't seem unreasonable for a few days in the summer. The whole thing -- I'm sorry it was scurrilous and it was rubbish that letter, and I was incensed by it, actually. I must say and now you remind me of it, I am again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay let's --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He quotes you as having said lawyers say the client is the enemy. Do you recall ever saying that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes I do. That was something some lawyer friend of mine in Latvia said that the senior partner of their firm told the juniors always remember the client is the enemy; but it was a jocular way of saying what we all know that clients lack judgement about their own case and you have to restrain them and you have to override them sometimes with your own judgement. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So he misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I -- whether he misunderstood me, I think is rather charitable to say he misunderstood me. He misrepresented me in his letter, whether he truly misunderstood me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm going to AD2 which is a statement by --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Which the rest of the stuff in his letter is rubbish as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go to a statement of Stefan Karganovic, who I understand was your case manager from April 2005 to May 2006.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. April, May, yes, that's right; yeah, yeah, April May 2006 yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He also makes the allegation that you were fairly uninterested in the historical and factual background of the case. How would you respond to that comment?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Same answer, I think. I was interested enough -- as a matter of fact, Mr. Krajisnik, as far as I remember, Mr. Krajisnik who legitimately or not didn't hesitate to be critical, why shouldn't he given what was at stake for him; but I don't remember Mr. Krajisnik being particularly critical about that, certainly not when it came to his own evidence, he was rather complimentary about my cross with things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And on the witnesses who offered political evidence was Mr. Krajisnik heavily involved in the preparation for their cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Examination?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I don't think -- we never refused to go see Mr. Krajisnik either, if I remember. I'm not saying absolutely never, after all there might have been odd days; but we made ourselves available to him and he to us, I will compliment him on that even though it's his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There's a suggestion that the Defence during the time of Stefan Karganovic could be best described as improvisation?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That certainly describes Mr. Karganovic's work, but the -- a lot of it -- he was a first-class interpreter and translator, by the way. No question about it, about the best that I've come across, Mr. Karganovic, but it's improvisation. I've -- I've described the way the case was. If that's intended to be a description of what I've described, then it's correct. If it's intended to be something different, then it's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Let's move on to Exhibit AD4 which you have in front of you, the letter to Mr. Zahar --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- and the attachment which is in that exhibit. What do you recall the -- to be the circumstances under which you prepared this letter?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Tremendous castigation of the Defence team by Judge Orie publicly and in court orders which in one case was gratuitously renamed to -- from the application in order to contain a direct disparagement of the Defence, when in fact we were -- we were really working hard, and we were really doing, I felt in the circumstances, a good job in very difficult circumstances, and I felt given what had been impose on us. The end of the Prosecution case was an absolute nightmare, the last couple of months, June, July 2005, absolute nightmare; and as I recall it here Chrissa Loukas had left the case exhausted and had been exhausted even before she'd finished on the case. We had Mr. Josse as new counsel. We were -- we were struggling, and we were doing our best, and it seemed not to be accepted that we were really trying hard. So those were the circumstances. We felt we weren't being listened to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: At any point during the course of your representation of Mr. Krajisnik did you consider that you could no longer represent his best interests and offer to resign the case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It wasn't an option because the -- when Chrissa Loukas applied to leave the case as early as October 2004, she wanted to go home. I mean she came back from the summer recess in 2004, and she wanted to go home to Australia, I mean; and the Registry made it perfectly clear it wasn't going to happen. They weren't going to contemplate any change of the counsel team. Eventually of course we did manage to organise a change and it took real difficulty, cost neutral for the Registry, organised that change which took a lot of work to Mr. Josse, but, no, I was -- the directive on assignment of Defence counsel does not allow me to resign. I also actually did say to Mr. Krajisnik quite early on when -- I think probably around the time that Chrissa Loukas put in her application I did say to him, "Mr. Krajisnik, I will stick with you to the end of this case."

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Because you viewed it as your professional obligation?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: And I wanted him to know because he had people wanting to leave, dropping away. He didn't like that. And I promised him that I would stay with him to the end of the case, and he took it in the right spirit. Actually, I've got to say Mr. Krajisnik was appreciative and always took that in the right spirit, and of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Let's just deal with one point that appears at page 7192, and it deals with the problem of the Defence as a result of Mr. Krajisnik not making his contribution to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It certainly had a -- it certainly had a negative impact. It -- it had to. But actually, I -- I said to the Registry, and I think I probably must have said it to the Trial Chamber at some stage that what this case really needed to be done at the pace at which the Trial Chamber eventually settled down to, what this case really needed was three counsel, or more than two let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you eventually get three counsel?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, we have to make a break. Is that an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, whatever pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So can we break now for 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing. I give the floor to Mr. Kremer to continue the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just a few more questions and then we'll go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just a few questions and then we'll return to open session. I'm referring to paragraph 9 of Mr. Karganovic's letter. I just want to -- I'll read you what he says and ask for your comment. He says: "It seemed that the Defence team did not have a plan according to which it operated, particularly in the phase when the Defence started to present its evidence and no longer just reacted to some moves of the Prosecution. The approach was more than -- more often than not experimental rather than functionally directed." How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you in fact have a plan according to which the Defence team operated when the Defence started?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did, and Mr. Josse is a very experienced counsel, and we -- we talked it through. I've got to say, we didn't really involve Mr. Karganovic in those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And when Mr. Mano was working as an intern was he involved in discussions about legal strategy, trial strategy?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Karganovic invited to meetings between you and Mr. Josse and the other legal assistants to talk about legal or trial strategy?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: We had. I've got to say -- I mean, Mr. Karganovic is a very affable member of the team. The team often met in all sorts of ways and of course we always -- not always but nearly always had Mr. Karganovic with us whenever we went to see Mr. Krajisnik, but I mean a huge amount of talking went on between Mr. Josse and me without anybody else there at all, as you'd expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karganovic told the Court during the course of his testimony that he had told both you and Chrissa Loukas that his inquiries in respect of the allegations being made -- or to be made to Mr. Davidovic were false; and notwithstanding his telling you that on the 27th of June, in the morning of the hearing in the afternoon Chrissa Loukas asked him questions regarding whether he had extorted money from a certain doctor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I remember a tremendous issue about the cross-examination of Mr. Davidovic by Ms. Loukas. I do. But what I don't remember -- I'm sorry, this is a suggestion that Chrissa Loukas already knew that the allegations were false before she put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you knew too. That's the allegation that Mr. Karganovic put to the Court last week.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's untrue. That's absolutely untrue. Well, in the sense that I'm absolutely sure it's untrue in relation to Chrissa Loukas, because unless she was completely lying to me about this particular issue, I'm absolutely confident that this is false in relation to Chrissa Loukas; and it's certainly false in relation to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go back into open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, can I be very clear because this is -- because after all, I know Mr. Karganovic gave his evidence in closed session; but this is a direct allegation by Mr. Karganovic that Chrissa Loukas, knowing that the information she was going to be putting to the witness was false nevertheless went ahead and -- and put it. Is that -- is that what Mr. Karganovic was saying? Can I -- I'm sorry if I'm repeating myself, but I'm rather startled. Is that how far it goes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That was my interpretation of it. Perhaps I can read you what Mr. Karganovic said. I'm now referring to 484, 485 of the transcript: "What specifically did you tell Ms. Loukas about your telephone conversation?" That's with the witness saying it was false: "I told Ms. Loukas that the doctor said that the extortion that was alleged on the part of Mr. Davidovic did not take place.
