The doctor denied the allegation that was made by Mr. Krajisnik's investigators. "All right. And were you present in court when the allegation was put to Mr. Davidovic about this fact? Is that correct? "I'm sure I was." And he then a question later on: "Did you tell Mr. Stewart that you were concerned about the cross-examination that was being actively objected to by the Prosecution continuing when you told her that the witness did not stand by the investigator's statement? "Answer: The Defence," meaning both Ms. Loukas and Mr. Stewart. "Were both aware of the outcome of my telephone conversation and the speculation was that Mr. Davidovic was such a powerful and intimidating figure that even though these people may not have been hurt by him, they did not dare to talk about it, so that was their view of it." Do you recall Mr. -- sharing that opinion with Ms. Loukas after you were made aware by Mr. Karganovic of the outcome of his telephone call?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No. I -- I don't. I -- I -- I did at the time. I'm sorry, I really do not remember all the details and ins and outs, but at the time it was a very big issue; and I did speak very specifically to Chrissa Loukas about it. The Trial Chamber were very concerned about it. I came to the conclusion that although -- and I'll bluntly put it this way: Although Chrissa Loukas's cross-examination had gone right up to the line on what really could very punctually and very directly be put to the witness, it hadn't crossed it; and I think the idea that -- that -- what I seem to be reading here is the idea that Mr. Karganovic was some monitor of ethical standards, some protector of ethical standards, which the other two of us, Ms. Loukas and me failed to meet, well that's just not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm going to put it to you simply, sir. Did Mr. Karganovic tell you that the result of his telephone inquiry was that the witness who is alleged to have been the subject or the victim of the extortion by Mr. Davidovic had said that the allegation was false? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: On the 27th of June --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- 2004 before the witness testified?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm sure he didn't. There was a lot of discussion afterwards, and I do remember becoming very unhappy about the reliability of the information acquired by Mr. Karganovic. I -- I had been, and I -- what Chrissa Loukas put to the witness, it merited investigation to see where we'd gone with the results that I've said, but -- but the -- the idea that we were told this in advance in this way and nevertheless went ahead, no, I don't -- I don't remember the dates and so on, but I -- no, I don't accept that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, just getting to -- getting back to sort of the Defence strategy that you implemented, there were a couple of points that I want to add to the list of areas that are part -- were part of the Defence strategy during the Prosecution case and also during the Defence case and that was an attempt to show that Mr. Krajisnik had no knowledge of the crimes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And another was an attempt to show that Mr. Krajisnik, A, that there was no common plan and no criminal plan or -- and that Mr. Krajisnik was not part of it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, ultimately you did file a final trial brief in this proceeding, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And all of the issues that were part of the Defence strategy were covered in your final trial brief both in terms of attacking the Prosecution portrayal of those issues and in showing why the Defence portrayal was to be preferred?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I just want to confirm a few points about joint criminal enterprise or JCE. When you accepted the case, you understood that one of the central planks, I think is the word used in your opening statement, of the Prosecution case against Mr. Krajisnik was, in fact, the theory of joint criminal enterprise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, on the footing that I must have read the indictment before I accepted the case. The answer is yes. I don't think I'd had ever heard much about joint criminal enterprise before that in my life, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Before you started the trial in February of 2004, did you fully familiarise yourself with the legal concept of joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly did that, and Chrissa Loukas did it as well because after we were able to do that without getting any papers from Mr. Brashich it's -- of course we were. We had -- of course we had the indictment. It wasn't that we could do nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And so some of the time spent in the early stages while you were waiting for the papers was doing the legal research and the legal thinking necessary to deal with some of the interconnected factual challenges that you were expecting to meet later on in the case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: In the very early stages, I mean, in a way it was almost all we could do; but, in fact, it would have been a perfectly logical, sensible thing to do anyway at that stage as one of the first things I'm quite sure for both of us although Chrissa was a very experienced criminal lawyer. I think that JCE as we know it here was a new animal to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't think you've answered my question. Did you do it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, beg your pardon, yes we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And so you were aware then of the elements of the mode of JCE liability when cross-examining Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in your final trial brief you argued both the JCE in the form pleaded is not an appropriate mode of liability in this case and the conditions for liability under JCE have not been met in the case.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and we had some extra brains on the matter by that time. We had Ms. Butler, Michelle Butler, who was certainly a serious brain; and we had and some very, very good intern working with us. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in fact Ms. Butler joined the Defence team in September of 2005?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And she -- approximately?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And she recruited some interns to assist in drafting of the final trial brief?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. They put together -- they analysed and they put together material for that purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And on the subject of JCE, the trial brief has a section from pages 39 to 58 dealing with the subject?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I'll take your word for the numbers, yes. It's -- yes, of course it has a section, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was Mr. Karganovic ever asked to participate in the -- in any discussions where JCE was discussed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that, but I very much doubt it, to be frank. I very much doubt it. He wasn't even on the case, of course, by the time we got to the final brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: He'd left some months before. No, I really don't think so, unless he just happened to be in the room, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: During the course of your Defence of Mr. Krajisnik, do you think that at any point you did not fulfil your professional obligation to protect his best interests as a client?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No. My professional obligation just pained to do my best. No, I don't feel I -- sorry. I feel I did fulfil my professional obligation, yes. I should say, sorry, just looking and being very analytical, of course, my professional obligation isn't just to do my best, it's that my best should be good enough; and so I want to be absolutely clear. I believe I did my best and I believe my best with my team did fulfil our professional obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And at the end of this case, it's my understanding that Mr. Krajisnik asked that you and Mr. Josse be added to the list of people who were to assist him on appeal. Do you remember having any discussions with Mr. Krajisnik about working on his appeal?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not sure that -- I don't remember that I was to be added to that list. I thought I wasn't, actually, but perhaps my memory's playing me tricks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I think Mr. Josse certainly was because Mr. Josse has, in fact, assisted in -- whether it's Mr. Nicholls' team or since he became amicus curiae or when he was Mr. Krajisnik counsel, I don't know; but he's certainly been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Mr. Krajisnik was a very difficult client during the course of the trial. On at least one occasion Mr. Krajisnik sought to self-represent.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I don't blame him for being difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: But he was. I mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Ultimately a compromise was met or reached with the Trial Chamber and he was permitted to ask questions with the leave of the Chamber of Prosecution witnesses and also of Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah. That was very unsatisfactory. The -- I -- it was very unsatisfactory. I, as counsel, and I was after all counsel throughout, I did not consider it in Mr. Krajisnik's interests to have that right because he would exercise it. I must say bluntly, Your Honours, that the circumstances in which that arose, as far as I remember, related to the evidence of Mr. Bjelobrk and the reasons for Mr. Krajisnik being given that right, I -- in my view are not correct and proper reasons. What happened was that we needed more time -- this is my recollection, it's the best I can do: We needed more time to -- for Mr. Krajisnik to instruct me to complete cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk; and what I remember was that the Trial Chamber then suggested at some point, well, if Mr. Krajisnik knows all this detail, then why doesn't he take over some of the cross-examination, and I objected to that; and that was an improper reason for sidestepping counsel and giving the client the right to ask questions. It was -- it was -- in fact, it fitted the whole approach because it was designed to save time, and I think specifically to let Mr. Bjelobrk if possible finish his evidence on a Friday, although I believe he did come back later. It was in my view quite an improper reason for doing it. It was an unfair decision because it was -- it was obvious that Mr. Krajisnik would take advantage of it for which I don't blame him, but it was going to be against his interests. It also, and I expressed this to Mr. Harhoff, one thing that I felt rather annoyed about was it caused enormous conflict between Mr. Krajisnik and me as it was bound to do, and it was -- it was extremely unhelpful, as I did tell Mr. Harhoff specifically of course with a view to him passing it on. It was extremely unhelpful and caused absolutely unnecessary conflict between Mr. Krajisnik and me; and it was absolutely contrary to his interests. And by the way I sought specific advice from the ADC, the Association of Defence Counsel and my own bar in England and received an endorsement from both of my position in continuing to object to the Trial Chamber's position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you did object?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I did object. I objected consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't going to stand up every morning and object, but my objections were overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. In terms of the material you've mentioned on several occasions you had a very strong team at the end.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And during the course of the Defence case, would it be fair to say that the team was strong as well?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: It varied. It's bound to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. Is it fair to say that during the course of the Defence case there were not the same crises or difficulties that you experienced as a Defence team during the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think to be fair there weren't really quite the same strings. I think that has to be acknowledged. I think the strains at certain points -- not points. The strains at certain points in the Prosecution case, the physical strains, the demands were heavier, and we were given some extra money as well in the last few months of the case. But, yes, the team varied, and you're quite right the team we had right at the very end, although small, was, I felt, very high quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Can you point to any part -- any witness in the Prosecution case where you feel that your cross-examination was inadequate professionally?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I haven't done the exercise of picking over the transcripts to see whether my own -- analyse to see whether my own cross-examination was inadequate. Well, the answer is I haven't, no, but I haven't attempted the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And have you attempted the exercise for the cross-examinations done by Chrissa Loukas or Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So you're not able to point to a single witness where you can say that the cross-examination that was either curtailed or ineffective because of failure or lack of time to prepare, lack of ability to review documents had an impact?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, no because I haven't done the exercise, but I think when one looks at the transcript one can see times I protested then we were not given enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik -- I'm sorry, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not hearing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm going back to your reasons for not requesting an adjournment, a point about which Mr. Nicholls examined you. Do I recollect right your net position this way, that you might have reasons now as you sit there to question some of the decisions you took in the past; but that at the time, in view of all the circumstances known to you, those decisions then taken represented your honest, professional judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you one other question, that is this: You remember the bit about not more than 15 per cent of the overall material having been read? Now, I don't have the material in front of me, but I recall this -- this much, that that was a statement attributed to you and not to your team. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense I -- I think I was -- and then it seemed that I was interrupting. I was going to raise the question maybe it was an hour ago as to when that point was put to me is whether what I had said was that I had not read or my team and that was exactly -- Your Honour has it, that was exactly a question I was raising, but then it got passed over. I beg your pardon, Your Honour. So the question now is whether -- whether I -- whether I was saying I had not read more than 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if I said it I said it when I said it. I can't say that I would have any useful recollection now of the precise position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I collect your meaning this way, that you were saying that you had not read more than 15 per cent of the material, that you were not saying that your team had read not more than 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what I said, but actually as far as the recollection is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question would be this: Who examined Mr. Krajisnik? You said he gave evidence for 40 days, and 23 of those days were spent on the examination-in-chief. Who examined him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did most of it. Mr. Josse did -- I don't know whether it was two, three days or something like that much more. Mr. Josse dealt specifically with intercepts. It might not be absolutely the only thing he dealt with, but a small number of days were set aside when Mr. Josse dealt with intercepts but it was -- the bulk of it was me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, replying to Mr. Kremer a few months ago I understood that you said that you did not know of any instance of cross-examination by you or by Mrs. Loukas, which suffered from lack of time or from inadequate preparation. I must say I have the impression and I will have to look at the transcript that in answering the Judges' question later, earlier today, your answer was quite different. I had the impression that you said that your cross-examination did suffer at least from the fact that you were not given adequate time and you had to curtail your cross-examination on matters of importance. Could you at set me right on this seeming contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't see a contradiction. I'm being asked whether I can point to specific witnesses and specific examples; and the answer is: No, I can't. By name, no I can't because I had not been reading the trial transcript of all my cross-examinations. Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't see a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: As a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You maintain what you said earlier today that you cross-examinations did suffer or they did not suffer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, they did. I knew at the time. I can remember without being able to name the particular witnesses, we were well aware on many occasions that our cross-examinations were suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the significance of your answer to Mr. Kremer is simply that you cannot speak specifically to one particular cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's because the trial finished two years ago, and I have not made it my business to read the trial transcripts of the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So as a general proposition you maintain what you said earlier, but I cannot point to specific cases. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour has it a hundred per cent right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, you can re-examine the witness and you have 20 minutes to do so. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, on several occasions we heard you say today, let me just give you a couple of examples, that you did not have enough time to prepare and as you said you had to put out the brush fires as you went along; and by way of an example, at page 35 and page 36 of today's transcript you said that you did not have enough time to examine crucial witnesses and this pertained for the most part to Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Djeric, their examination. Now I have a question for you. Today the Prosecutor put to you what you wanted to do, to separate Krajisnik from the crime base because you considered that there was no link between him and the direct perpetrators, that he was not a member of the Presidency, that he was not a member of the joint criminal enterprise, and that he was nothing but the president of the Assembly and a member of the negotiating team. Now, my question to you is: This lack of time, the fact that you did not have the capability to prepare properly, was that one of the reasons why you fail to prove what you wanted to prove in your case? And Mr. Kremer provided us with specifics, and now I just pinpointed some of the things that you wanted to do, that you planned to do.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kiseljak, I'm sorry, I -- Your Honours, I can't say in the end what were the reasons, given the burden of proof's on the Prosecution, but ultimately I can't say what were the reasons why we failed to prove what we wanted to prove. That -- there seems to be much more involved in that, Your Honours, than questions of time. It's a question of the actual evidence, and I don't feel that Your Honours would wish me to get into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I hope that the Appeals Chamber will take a position on the weight or to what extent the lack of time led to your inability to carry out the tasks that you assigned to yourself. Now I have three brief questions. I hope I will be able to ask questions directly, because there is a misunderstanding, and that pertains to Davidovic and Mr. Karganovic. I would like to remind you to the trial -- of the trial. Do you recall what was the basis for the examination by Chrissa Loukas of Mr. Davidovic in which she actually accused him of having extorted somebody?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: I've got to say, Mr. Krajisnik, I do not have a detail recollection of this. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you now that Ms. Loukas had in front of her a statement prepared by the investigators does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what I remember is that -- that when I did as I said I did, I did specifically inquire. It was my responsibility to do that given the furor which had arisen. As lead counsel, I had to do that. All I can say is that when I did look into it with Ms. Loukas particularly I reach the conclusion as I described in my answers to Mr. Kremer's questions, but I don't remember now the details, I'm afraid and even refreshment of my memory is, I think, not going to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Fair enough. One more question. I hope that I will have no more than one or two questions. The Prosecutor today put a fact to you, reminded you of the fact that Krajisnik prepared a lot of materials for you and presented those materials to you, and now I would like to ask you this: It was impossible for us to communicate directly because I don't speak English and, Mr. Stewart, you don't speak Serbian.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Were the negotiating resources a bottleneck -- or, rather, the interpretation resources, was that a bottleneck that prevented everything that I had prepared from being presented to you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it was inevitably a frustration for you, and it is inevitably and it was inevitably an extra element of the work that we had to do. So that whether it was Ms. Cmeric when she was the case manager, and she was really more than a case manager; she was terrific in all sorts of ways, whether it was Mr. Sladojevic later for whom you know I have the absolute highest regard, the material had to go through them. They are very good, very intelligent people. They did some sifting, Mr. Krajisnik. They didn't simply pass on everything you did. They'd still be translating now. That's a slight exaggeration, of course, but it would have taken them a very long time. But your material was considered, Mr. Krajisnik, it was. It was done as a way it should be through a team. It was done by going through the various members of the team in a suitably delegated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And my last question: You mentioned here and, well, this is a fact, that I testified for 40 days. Do you think that the testimony by the accused could have rectified the disparity between the number of witnesses called by the Prosecution and those called by the Defence, or was this done out of a necessity because we could not prepare the appropriate number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, was -- was calling you as a witness done out of necessity? Is that -- is that your question? I'm not clear. I'm sorry, perhaps I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question now.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you consider that calling the accused to testify, he proceeded to testify for 40 days, could it have made up for the disparity between the number of witnesses called by the Prosecution and witnesses called by the Defence which did not manage to prepare a larger number of witnesses, if I may add that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I think the best way I can answer that question you -- you made it absolutely clear right from the outset that you were going to give evidence. I think I would take it that whatever the ultimate value of your evidence in broad terms, the accused himself is worth quite a lot of other witnesses because inevitably you had and have very considerable knowledge of the subjects at hand, so the -- if you're balancing on the scales, yes, you must have been -- how it would work out for you was another matter, but you might have been worth quite name of witnesses, yes. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much, and I would like to give back to you the five minutes that you've gifted me at the beginning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Well, this concludes the examination of the witness. Mr. Stewart, the Appeals Chamber thanks you for giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And you may be excused now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: This -- this also concludes this evidentiary hearing. The Appeals Chamber will now rise. The hearing's adjourned.
